AWS Certified CloudOps Engineer – Associate (SOA-C03)

Learn symptom → evidence → control → verified result. Follow a two-AZ workload, compare the closest alternatives, then practise the deciding constraint. Cards contain service features, small examples and AWS references.

Checked: 10 November 2026. Scope follows the SOA-C03 guide and revisions. Exercises are local simulations; no AWS account is needed.

Operating model · Deciding constraint · Service cards · Six labs · Practice · Coverage · Architecture explorer

1. Understand the operating environment

Provision → operate → observe → investigate → remediate → recover. Select a responsibility, then reveal the AWS services. Workload traffic, changes and evidence are separate flows.

ARCHITECTURE BEFORE SERVICESOne workload. Find the boundary that owns the symptom.

Provisioning changes the environment; users exercise it; evidence guides a bounded repair. Recovery succeeds only when the service and its data are validated. These are logical handoffs, not one packet travelling through every box.

Operating sequenceApplication traffic / dataConfiguration / corrective actionMonitoring evidence / feedback
All responsibilities · static reading
Provision / configure

Review the intended resource configuration and artifact before an operational change.

Dependencies. Versioned template, image, role, quota and free subnet IPs.

Failure. A deployment fails or creates drift from intended state.

Evidence. Stack events, change set, image/task status and CloudTrail actor.

Verify. Fix the prerequisite, complete rollback/reconcile and verify deployed state.

Operate

Keep the workload serving within its availability, latency and cost constraints.

Dependencies. Healthy targets, runtime identity, database, storage and network.

Failure. Instance running but unhealthy, or insufficient surviving capacity.

Evidence. Target health, scaling activities, guest metrics and DB load.

Verify. Restore usable capacity and verify the same user path under representative load.

Observe

Collect the metrics, logs, traces and relevant resource/API events needed to distinguish failures.

Dependencies. Agent/instrumentation, permissions, dimensions, retention and cross-account links.

Failure. An alarm has no data or the useful log/trace was never collected.

Evidence. Publication timestamps, alarm history, log streams and collection errors.

Verify. Repair collection, send a known test event and verify both evidence and alert delivery.

Investigate

Trace symptom → affected scope → evidence → likely cause. Identify the first boundary with a proven fault.

Dependencies. Correct account, Region, AZ, time window, principal and request correlation.

Failure. Treating a correlation or assistant recommendation as a confirmed cause.

Evidence. Logs/trace timing, API changes, configuration history and service health.

Verify. Choose a test that distinguishes the likely cause from the nearest alternative.

Remediate

Perform the smallest approved corrective action, with safe targeting, retries and rollback.

Dependencies. Scoped role, runbook, preconditions, approvals and concurrency/error limits.

Failure. A broad repair damages healthy resources or loops on its own events.

Evidence. Runbook step output, target API error and resulting resource state.

Verify. Confirm the exact action and retry safely; remove the cause, not just the symptom.

Validate / recover

Prove service and data recovery against actual RTO/RPO, then prevent recurrence.

Dependencies. Usable recovery point, KMS access, target network, dependency order and cutover plan.

Failure. Backup succeeds but restore, access or application cutover fails.

Evidence. Restore job, record checks, endpoint tests, elapsed outage and data age.

Verify. Verify business results and recovery objectives; record prevention in controlled configuration.

User request

Resolve a name, connect to the advertised endpoint and send the application request.

Dependencies. DNS response, client network, TLS trust and caller identity as required.

Failure. The name is wrong or a certificate does not match.

Evidence. DNS answers, served certificate and client-visible status/timing.

Verify. Retest from the affected source and account for DNS caches.

Route / filter

Apply cache/origin behaviour and listener routing to an eligible backend.

Dependencies. Routes, SG/NACL, return path, health check and target port.

Failure. A good DNS answer reaches a blocked or unhealthy target.

Evidence. Access/WAF/flow logs and target-health reason.

Verify. Correct the first failed hop and verify request plus response.

Application

Use the deployed artifact and runtime identity to process the request and construct a response.

Dependencies. CPU, memory, dependencies, role permissions, configuration and state.

Failure. A bad rollout, exhausted resource or denied downstream request.

Evidence. Version, logs, traces, utilisation, failed API action and status checks.

Verify. Rollback or repair the measured dependency; verify latency, errors and business outcome.

Durable state

Preserve the authoritative data and independent recoverable history.

Dependencies. Storage performance, database consistency, backups, encryption and access.

Failure. Slow I/O, logical corruption, inaccessible key or unusable recovery point.

Evidence. DB waits, volume metrics, version/recovery timestamp and KMS errors.

Verify. Restore/tune the right layer and validate integrity before cutover.

2. Read the deciding constraint

Name the affected scope, operation, failure and evidence before changing anything. A timeout, AccessDenied and stale data need different investigations.

Distinction Deciding clue Start with
Metrics / logs / traces Trend / event detail / one slow request Dimensions and statistic / matching log / downstream spans.
Audit / configuration history Who changed it / what settings existed CloudTrail / Config timeline.
Availability / capacity / performance Keep serving / handle more / finish faster Healthy targets / scaling activity / first saturated dependency.
Backup / replication / failover Historical undo / another copy / service continuity Recovery point / replication lag / failover evidence.
RTO / RPO Maximum outage / tolerable data loss Measured recovery time / usable recovery timestamp.
Identity / permissions / network Who / allowed action / reachable path Trust and policies / SG, NACL, routes and DNS.

Restore service first; prevent recurrence next. API success is not proof of application recovery.

3. Connect theory to services

Use the decision tables, then open a card for features and an example. Optional exercises expand in place; examples are excerpts with illustrative identifiers.

Local exercises: Alarm evaluation · Failure capacity · RTO/RPO · Stack recovery · Encrypted access · Network path.

3.1 Monitoring & performance — 22%

Signal → correlated evidence → bounded repair → measured outcome

When the requirement is… Start with… Deciding boundary
Trend / threshold CloudWatch metrics + alarm Check dimensions, statistic, period and missing data.
Individual slow request Logs + trace Correlate the actual dependency; sampling may hide a trace.
API change / resource history CloudTrail / Config Actor and configuration are different evidence.
Sustained performance limit Compute, EBS, storage or DB metrics Fix the first saturated dependency; measure before resizing.
CloudWatch metrics & alarms Logs, queries & traces CloudTrail & change evidence EventBridge, SNS & remediation EC2 performance & capacity EBS performance & snapshots S3 operations & protection EFS, FSx & S3 Files Health & assisted investigation

Implementation notes

Collect before investigating. Cross-account observability needs regional source links; a dashboard alone does not establish them. Verify notification delivery and the repaired workload.

Optional exercise · Alarm evaluation

Think of an alarm as a rule over a time window. Change the data or missing-data policy and explain why the state changes.

Illustrative fixed-window calculation: no older datapoints, ingestion lag, premature-transition rules or namespace-specific exceptions. Real CloudWatch evaluates more conditions; inspect its state history.

For 70, 90, missing with a threshold above 80 and 2-of-3: one known breach is insufficient alone. Treating absence as breaching supplies the second breach; treating it as notBreaching does not.

3.2 Reliability & recovery — 22%

Healthy capacity → failure isolation → protected history → tested recovery

When the requirement is… Start with… Deciding boundary
Traffic growth Scaling + a proportional metric More instances cannot fix a saturated shared database by themselves.
Host/AZ failure Healthy targets + Multi-AZ dependencies Measure surviving capacity, not only instance count.
Logical deletion Version / snapshot / PITR restore A healthy replica may contain the same deletion.
Regional disaster Approved DR runbook Choose by tested RTO, RPO, cost and dependency readiness.
Auto Scaling & elasticity Load balancing & target health RDS, Aurora & database recovery DynamoDB scaling & recovery ElastiCache & cache operations AWS Backup & disaster recovery

Implementation notes

Test the restored data and application. Include permissions, networking, reconnection and endpoint cutover in the recovery clock; a replica can contain the same logical deletion.

Optional exercise · ASG failure capacity

The ASG sets the staffing target; the ALB routes to eligible workers. A surviving instance count does not prove enough usable capacity.

Assumes equal instance capacity of 100 requests/s and health convergence. Launches are eventual and can fail. ASG min/max and single-Region scope still apply; this is not a capacity reservation.

Actual 5 and desired 5 with +3 requests desired 8. Losing AZ A leaves 3 instances, or an illustrative 300 requests/s: below 400 requests/s demand until adequate capacity recovers.

Optional exercise · RTO / RPO

RTO is the outage clock; RPO is how far the recovered ledger may lag. Both constraints must be met.

The table uses assumed measured procedures, not universal AWS timings or guarantees. Listed order approximates increasing standby cost; actual costs differ. Live standby options here have no independent historical undo.

ProcedureAssumed RTOAssumed RPOCost boundary
Daily backup + restore180 min1,440 minLow standby cost
Continuous PITR + restore90 min5 minRetention + restore
Pilot light45 min5 minCore data running
Warm standby10 min1 minReduced stack running

At RTO 120 minutes and RPO 15 minutes, the assumed daily backup fails both constraints; the illustrated PITR procedure meets both. Validate real recovery before making the same claim.

3.3 Deployment & automation — 22%

Versioned definition → reviewed change → rollout → health gate → rollback / reconcile

When the requirement is… Start with… Deciding boundary
Preview infrastructure impact Change set / CDK diff Preview does not execute or guarantee success.
Rollback itself failed Repair prerequisite + continue rollback Reconcile skipped resources before the next update.
Maintain existing nodes Systems Manager Agent, identity and outbound connectivity are prerequisites.
Many accounts / Regions StackSets, RAM and trusted roles Deploying copies differs from sharing an existing resource.
CloudFormation & CDK lifecycle Images & deployment operations Systems Manager operations Multi-account operations EventBridge, SNS & remediation

Implementation notes

Pin versions, test a small target, limit rollout concurrency and retain rollback inputs. Verify the workload after the stack or runbook finishes.

Optional exercise · Stack recovery

A failed update and a failed rollback are different states. Repair the prerequisite before repeating the operation.

For UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED, fix the permission/resource problem and continue rollback. Once UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE, review a corrected change set before another deployment.

3.4 Security & compliance — 16%

Known principal → trusted session → permitted operation → protected data → compliance evidence

When the requirement is… Start with… Deciding boundary
Cannot assume role Caller policy + target trust Trust is not the role’s downstream permission policy.
Encrypted read denied Data access + KMS key access Key state/context/policy still apply.
Unapproved configuration Config evaluation + safe remediation An aggregator alone neither records nor repairs.
Finding needs action Match finding source to control Patch, restrict or investigate; verify the actual outcome.
IAM access investigation Multi-account operations Config & continuous compliance KMS, encryption & secrets ACM & encrypted connections Security findings & classification

Implementation notes

Check the principal, trust, action/resource policy and any restricting controls separately. Keep secrets out of investigation logs.

Optional exercise · IAM / KMS access

The resource permission and the key-use permission protect different boundaries. This example uses an IAM-enabled KMS key policy.

A valid role and S3 permission still cannot read this SSE-KMS object without the required KMS permission. Explicit denial wins even when other allows are present.

3.5 Networking & delivery — 18%

Name → route → filter → listener → target → return path

When the requirement is… Start with… Deciding boundary
Name fails; IP succeeds DNS / Resolver / delegation Changing SG rules does not repair a wrong DNS answer.
Timeout on a reachable name Routes + SG/NACL + listener Check response path and ephemeral ports too.
Private AWS API access Gateway or interface endpoint Endpoint policy limits access; it does not grant IAM permissions.
Wrong cached response CloudFront behaviour / cache key Lower TTL cannot correct a missing variation dimension.
VPC routes, subnets & filters Endpoints & private connectivity Route 53 & DNS operations CloudFront & Global Accelerator Network evidence & protection

Implementation notes

Trace the actual source, destination and return path. Compare NAT, endpoint and cross-AZ costs. A modelled reachable path still needs a real application test.

Optional exercise · Network path

A route is a road; an SG is a stateful gate; a NACL is a stateless checkpoint in each direction.

Simplified browser ↔ ALB path plus backend SG check; backend NACLs, OS listener and TLS are assumed correct. ALB → backend is a separate connection with its own source ephemeral port and return rules. Broad 1024–65535 examples are not every OS’s exact range.

browser:54321 → ALB:443 needs inbound destination 443; ALB:443 → browser:54321 needs outbound destination 54321 at the ALB subnet NACL. Stateful SGs track the allowed connection; NACLs do not.

4. Practise the boundary

72 original questions. Answer once, identify the deciding clue and reject the closest alternative. Multiple-answer questions state the required count; focused follow-ups do not predict exam frequency.

All 72 scenarios & explanations · static reference
1.1 · Missing guest metric

CPU metrics arrive, but an EC2 memory-utilisation alarm has no datapoints. What directly supplies the missing measurement?

  1. Enable detailed EC2 monitoring
  2. Configure CloudWatch Agent to publish memory usage
  3. Create a CloudTrail trail
  4. Lower the alarm threshold
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: Configure CloudWatch Agent to publish memory usage

Clue. The metric does not exist yet; frequency and threshold are secondary.

  • Enable detailed EC2 monitoring: Changes supported built-in metric frequency; it does not collect guest memory.
  • Configure CloudWatch Agent to publish memory usage: The agent reads the guest metric and publishes it with configured identity/network access.
  • Create a CloudTrail trail: Records AWS API activity, not guest memory usage.
  • Lower the alarm threshold: Cannot create missing datapoints.

Change the requirement. If CPU existed but five-minute publication was too coarse, detailed monitoring could be appropriate.

Analogy. Install a thermometer before setting its warning temperature.

CloudWatch metrics & alarms · Logs, queries & traces

1.1 · No-data policy

A continuously reporting heartbeat must alert when publishing stops. With no older real datapoints available, which setting makes missing periods count toward a metric alarm?

  1. notBreaching
  2. ignore
  3. breaching
  4. Disable alarm actions
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: breaching

Clue. Absence itself is the failure signal. Real evaluation can retrieve older data.

  • notBreaching: Treats missing values as good for evaluation.
  • ignore: Retains the existing state when missing data controls evaluation.
  • breaching: Substitutes breaching values when CloudWatch needs missing datapoints.
  • Disable alarm actions: Prevents notification, not data loss.

Change the requirement. For a sparse error-only metric where absence is normal, notBreaching may fit.

Analogy. A missed check-in should ring the bell, not count as a healthy check-in.

CloudWatch metrics & alarms

1.2 · Find the change

A security group became open just before an incident. Which evidence identifies the API caller and change time?

  1. CloudTrail management event
  2. EC2 CPU graph
  3. ALB access log
  4. AWS Config configuration timeline
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: CloudTrail management event

Clue. The question is who changed an AWS setting.

  • CloudTrail management event: Captures supported configuration API activity and caller identity.
  • EC2 CPU graph: Shows utilisation, not the actor changing a rule.
  • ALB access log: Records requests, not this administrative API operation.
  • AWS Config configuration timeline: Shows recorded resource settings and changes, but does not replace CloudTrail API caller evidence.

Change the requirement. If you needed the sequence of recorded rule configurations, Config history would help.

Analogy. Consult the change register to find the signatory.

CloudTrail & change evidence · Config & continuous compliance

1.2 · Matched but not repaired

An EventBridge rule matches stopped-instance events, but the Automation never starts. Select TWO first checks.

  1. Target invocation permissions and role trust
  2. FailedInvocations, retry/DLQ and target execution evidence
  3. Only retest the already-matching event pattern
  4. Remove the event pattern to match every event
  5. Increase retries without inspecting a permanent AccessDenied
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: Target invocation permissions and role trust; FailedInvocations, retry/DLQ and target execution evidence

Clue. Matching and target invocation are separate boundaries.

  • Target invocation permissions and role trust: The rule/target needs the appropriate invocation and assumption permissions.
  • FailedInvocations, retry/DLQ and target execution evidence: Distinguishes routing success from delivery or execution failure.
  • Only retest the already-matching event pattern: Confirms matching again but does not diagnose the failed target invocation.
  • Remove the event pattern to match every event: Broadens potentially unsafe actions without fixing target access or delivery.
  • Increase retries without inspecting a permanent AccessDenied: Retrying the same permission denial does not repair the policy.

Change the requirement. If the runbook started but failed inside a step, inspect its step output and target resource access.

Analogy. A ticket accepted by dispatch may still never reach the technician.

EventBridge, SNS & remediation · Systems Manager operations

1.3 · Disk bottleneck

An EC2 service has high EBS latency and queue depth while CPU and memory are healthy. Instance EBS bandwidth has headroom; gp2 burst balance is depleted. What is the most relevant change to evaluate?

  1. Enable detailed EC2 monitoring as the performance fix
  2. Create a snapshot as the primary latency fix
  3. Move to appropriately provisioned gp3 performance
  4. Increase only CPU cores
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: Move to appropriately provisioned gp3 performance

Clue. The exhausted resource is volume I/O, with instance bandwidth ruled out.

  • Enable detailed EC2 monitoring as the performance fix: Improves metric frequency but does not add the missing volume I/O capacity.
  • Create a snapshot as the primary latency fix: Protects recovery state rather than provisioning sustained volume performance.
  • Move to appropriately provisioned gp3 performance: Separates volume performance from capacity; benchmark the required IOPS/throughput.
  • Increase only CPU cores: Evidence points to the volume, not CPU.

Change the requirement. If the instance EBS bandwidth were saturated, changing only volume IOPS would be insufficient.

Analogy. A faster loading dock helps only when the road to it has spare capacity.

EBS performance & snapshots · EC2 performance & capacity

1.3 · Database wait evidence

Writer transaction latency rises with lock waits on a few SQL statements; storage and CPU have headroom. What should you investigate first?

  1. SQL, transaction duration and lock contention with Database Insights
  2. Double every EC2 web instance
  3. Add RDS Proxy without investigating transaction locks
  4. Add a read replica and leave blocking writer transactions unchanged
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: SQL, transaction duration and lock contention with Database Insights

Clue. Wait type identifies a database concurrency issue.

  • SQL, transaction duration and lock contention with Database Insights: Directly addresses the measured wait.
  • Double every EC2 web instance: Can increase database pressure without fixing locks.
  • Add RDS Proxy without investigating transaction locks: Connection pooling does not remove the demonstrated blocking writer transactions.
  • Add a read replica and leave blocking writer transactions unchanged: Read scaling does not directly fix the lock contention on the writer.

Change the requirement. If connection setup rather than lock waits dominated, RDS Proxy/connection pooling could be relevant.

Analogy. More checkout lanes do not help when one transaction holds the only storeroom key.

RDS, Aurora & database recovery

1.3 · Shared-file operating boundary

Two Linux application instances in separate AZs need concurrent access to the same persistent files. Which option directly fits?

  1. Regional EFS with mount targets and permitted NFS access
  2. One EBS volume attached across both AZs
  3. Two instance-store directories
  4. Only a CloudFront distribution
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: Regional EFS with mount targets and permitted NFS access

Clue. The required interface is shared files across AZs, not independent block disks.

  • Regional EFS with mount targets and permitted NFS access: Provides supported shared NFS access across AZs; check DNS and mount security.
  • One EBS volume attached across both AZs: EBS attachments cannot cross AZ boundaries.
  • Two instance-store directories: They are separate local ephemeral storage, not a shared persistent filesystem.
  • Only a CloudFront distribution: Caches HTTP content; it is not the requested shared application filesystem.

Change the requirement. For Windows SMB/AD semantics, consider an appropriate FSx deployment.

Analogy. Choose a shared filing room rather than two independent desk drawers.

EFS, FSx & S3 Files · EBS performance & snapshots

1.3 · Replica writes: default versus exception

An RDS MySQL read replica normally rejects writes. An engineer says no write can ever succeed before promotion. Which correction is accurate?

  1. read_only=0 can permit writes, but conflicting changes can break replication
  2. Any replica write is safe once read_only=0
  3. Its endpoint automatically redirects writes to the source
  4. Changing max_allowed_packet makes it a writable primary
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: read_only=0 can permit writes, but conflicting changes can break replication

Clue. Distinguish normally prohibited writes from a documented parameter-controlled exception.

  • read_only=0 can permit writes, but conflicting changes can break replication: The default is a control, not an absolute physical impossibility; replica-specific indexes are a documented special case.
  • Any replica write is safe once read_only=0: Permitting a write does not protect replication from conflicting application changes.
  • Its endpoint automatically redirects writes to the source: The replica has its own endpoint; do not assume transparent write routing.
  • Changing max_allowed_packet makes it a writable primary: Message-size limits do not change the replica’s role or consistency model.

Change the requirement. If independent application writes are required, use an appropriate writer architecture rather than exploiting a read-replica exception.

Analogy. Removing a desk’s read-only sign does not make two clerks’ conflicting ledger edits safe.

RDS, Aurora & database recovery

1.3 · Replication breaks only on a large message

MySQL replication works until a large logical message arrives. The source allows a larger max_allowed_packet than the replica. What should be checked first?

  1. Matching appropriate source/replica parameter values and the failing message
  2. The total number of stored database rows
  3. Only aggregate writes per minute
  4. The VPC MTU as if max_allowed_packet were a TCP frame size
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: Matching appropriate source/replica parameter values and the failing message

Clue. The error identifies message size, not capacity or overall transaction throughput.

  • Matching appropriate source/replica parameter values and the failing message: The smaller receiving limit can reject a sufficiently large logical message.
  • The total number of stored database rows: Database size does not define this individual-message limit.
  • Only aggregate writes per minute: A rate is not the logical size limit that the error identifies.
  • The VPC MTU as if max_allowed_packet were a TCP frame size: MySQL logical messages and network frames are different units.

Change the requirement. If the error instead identifies a conflicting local replica write, parameter matching will not repair that inconsistency.

Analogy. A letterbox opening limits one envelope, not the total size of the archive.

RDS, Aurora & database recovery

1.3 · Busy device name after detach

Evidence identifies a guest driver retaining a device mapping after detach; the EBS volume is otherwise available in the correct AZ. What should be evaluated next?

  1. An unused supported attachment name, after checking actual guest mappings
  2. More gp2 burst credits
  3. A cross-AZ attachment to avoid the name
  4. Format the first disk whose name looks similar
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: An unused supported attachment name, after checking actual guest mappings

Clue. The question supplies a specific driver-name cause; do not infer it from every stuck attachment.

  • An unused supported attachment name, after checking actual guest mappings: The identified collision concerns naming/mapping, not disk I/O performance.
  • More gp2 burst credits: Credits affect performance, not resolution of this device-name collision.
  • A cross-AZ attachment to avoid the name: EBS attachment must remain in the volume’s AZ.
  • Format the first disk whose name looks similar: Names may be remapped; identify the actual volume before touching its data.

Change the requirement. For a different error such as attachment-count limit, use that control rather than repeatedly renaming devices.

Analogy. Two devices cannot claim the same reserved label merely because the storage service calls one available.

EBS performance & snapshots

1.3 · Resize a public EBS-backed instance

A compatible EBS-backed On-Demand instance has an auto-assigned public IPv4 and no EIP. Which TWO effects should an operator plan for during an in-place type change?

  1. Stop/change/start downtime
  2. The auto-assigned public IPv4 normally changes
  3. The instance ID and private IPv4 must always be replaced
  4. Instance-store contents are safely retained across the stop
  5. ASG membership can never interfere with planned stopping
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: Stop/change/start downtime; The auto-assigned public IPv4 normally changes

Clue. In-place change preserves identity differently from replacement, but needs downtime and address planning.

  • Stop/change/start downtime: Changing the type through this workflow requires stopping the instance.
  • The auto-assigned public IPv4 normally changes: An Elastic IP would have different address persistence.
  • The instance ID and private IPv4 must always be replaced: Those normally persist through ordinary stop/start of the same instance.
  • Instance-store contents are safely retained across the stop: Instance-store data is lost; EBS persistence is a different mechanism.
  • ASG membership can never interfere with planned stopping: An ASG can mark the stopped instance unhealthy and replace it.

Change the requirement. With an EIP, its public address can remain associated; a controlled replacement rollout has a different availability plan.

Analogy. The same named machine can reboot on another host while its temporary street number changes.

EC2 performance & capacity · Auto Scaling & elasticity

1.3 · Legacy network-interface bottleneck

Measurements identify a legacy EC2 virtual network interface as the bottleneck. General application networking is required, not tightly coupled MPI/HPC. Which path should be evaluated?

  1. Compatible enhanced networking/ENA and the exact instance’s bandwidth/PPS limits
  2. EFA as the universal answer to every packet-rate issue
  3. Direct Connect as if it replaced the guest instance NIC
  4. A universal 20K-PPS or 25-Gbps ceiling for all modern EC2
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: Compatible enhanced networking/ENA and the exact instance’s bandwidth/PPS limits

Clue. The workload and measured constraint identify ordinary enhanced networking, not a different network product.

  • Compatible enhanced networking/ENA and the exact instance’s bandwidth/PPS limits: Targets the identified interface capability and measured resource limits.
  • EFA as the universal answer to every packet-rate issue: EFA serves specialised tightly coupled communication requirements.
  • Direct Connect as if it replaced the guest instance NIC: It supplies hybrid connectivity, not a replacement for this interface capability.
  • A universal 20K-PPS or 25-Gbps ceiling for all modern EC2: Legacy exam figures are not per-type modern guarantees.

Change the requirement. For tightly coupled HPC communication, EFA compatibility and application support could become relevant.

Analogy. Choose the correct vehicle interface before buying a different intercity road.

EC2 performance & capacity · Network evidence & protection

1.2 · New launch API versus instance start

Notify an SNS subscriber when a matching new EC2 launch API operation occurs, including while prior notifications are still being processed. What is the clearest event path?

  1. CloudTrail RunInstances event → EventBridge rule → SNS
  2. Any EC2 running state event, assumed to identify creation uniquely
  3. One metric alarm held in ALARM for every matching event
  4. CloudTrail is mandatory for every EventBridge service event
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: CloudTrail RunInstances event → EventBridge rule → SNS

Clue. The operation identity is RunInstances; a state name alone is ambiguous.

  • CloudTrail RunInstances event → EventBridge rule → SNS: Matches the launch operation; configure the appropriate trail/event and target permissions.
  • Any EC2 running state event, assumed to identify creation uniquely: Starting an existing instance can also produce running transitions.
  • One metric alarm held in ALARM for every matching event: State-transition notification is not one notification per repeated event.
  • CloudTrail is mandatory for every EventBridge service event: EventBridge can also receive direct service events without CloudTrail.

Change the requirement. If the requirement is per created instance rather than per API call, extract/process every instance ID from a multi-instance launch event.

Analogy. Use the new-order receipt rather than every later “order now active” status change.

EventBridge, SNS & remediation · CloudTrail & change evidence

1.1 · Test the journey without real users

Operations needs scheduled browser/API checks with managed metrics and test artifacts even when no customers are active. Which capability most directly fits?

  1. CloudWatch Synthetics canary
  2. ServiceLens / trace map alone
  3. A dashboard alone
  4. Only a scheduled Lambda invocation, assuming all canary reporting exists automatically
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: CloudWatch Synthetics canary

Clue. The requirement is active synthetic execution plus managed evidence, not passive correlation.

  • CloudWatch Synthetics canary: Purpose-built scheduled synthetic tests with monitoring integrations and artifacts.
  • ServiceLens / trace map alone: Correlates observed telemetry; it does not execute the endpoint test.
  • A dashboard alone: Displays existing signals rather than generating test requests.
  • Only a scheduled Lambda invocation, assuming all canary reporting exists automatically: Custom Lambda can run checks, but monitoring/reporting/artifacts must be assembled appropriately.

Change the requirement. If a bespoke unsupported test executor is required, scheduled custom execution with explicit instrumentation may fit.

Analogy. A mystery shopper creates a test visit; a CCTV index only helps inspect visits already recorded.

CloudWatch metrics & alarms · Logs, queries & traces · EventBridge, SNS & remediation

1.3 · Resize an EBS-root host with scratch data

A compatible EBS-root EC2 instance also has important temporary results on instance store. It needs more RAM by in-place resizing. What should operations expect?

  1. Resize by editing AMI metadata without stopping
  2. Detach and move instance store to the larger host
  3. A normal reboot and a stop/start erase the same storage
  4. Copy required scratch data out, then stop/change type/start with downtime
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: Copy required scratch data out, then stop/change type/start with downtime

Clue. Root storage is EBS, while additional scratch storage has a different lifecycle.

  • Resize by editing AMI metadata without stopping: The running instance’s compute configuration is not changed by editing an image definition.
  • Detach and move instance store to the larger host: Instance-store volumes cannot be detached and transferred like EBS volumes.
  • A normal reboot and a stop/start erase the same storage: Normal reboot preserves instance-store data; stop/start does not.
  • Copy required scratch data out, then stop/change type/start with downtime: EBS-root resizing uses stop/start; EBS data persists, but instance-store data does not.

Change the requirement. An instance-store-root workload needs migration rather than this normal resize path.

Analogy. A persistent filing cabinet and a temporary workbench have different moving rules.

EC2 performance & capacity · EBS performance & snapshots

1.1 · Shard quota warning is not a latency trace

Operations needs supported checks warning about Kinesis shard-count quota utilisation, with a notification on check status changes. Which approach fits?

  1. Treat Trusted Advisor results as guaranteed real-time delivery
  2. Trusted Advisor → eligible EventBridge integration in us-east-1 → SNS
  3. ServiceLens automatically detects the 80% quota threshold
  4. Watch only IncomingBytes to determine allocated shard-count quota
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: Trusted Advisor → eligible EventBridge integration in us-east-1 → SNS

Clue. The requirement concerns quota allocation and check status, not one request’s latency.

  • Treat Trusted Advisor results as guaranteed real-time delivery: Checks can lag and the EventBridge delivery is best effort; plan eligibility applies.
  • Trusted Advisor → eligible EventBridge integration in us-east-1 → SNS: The supported quota check uses environment usage snapshots and check-status events.
  • ServiceLens automatically detects the 80% quota threshold: Trace correlation investigates observed application telemetry, not every AWS quota recommendation.
  • Watch only IncomingBytes to determine allocated shard-count quota: Data throughput is different from the number of allocated shards against an account quota.

Change the requirement. Producer throttling or a hot shard instead requires throughput/error metrics and partition-key investigation.

Analogy. A building occupancy inspection is different from timing each service desk.

Health & assisted investigation · CloudWatch metrics & alarms · EventBridge, SNS & remediation

1.1 · The image has the agent, but telemetry is missing

A new ASG member boots from an AMI containing the configured CloudWatch Agent. EC2 built-in CPU metrics appear but guest memory metrics do not. What should be checked?

  1. Assume ASG reinstalls and starts every agent automatically
  2. Enable detailed monitoring to create the missing memory metric
  3. Use the original image-source host’s metrics as proof
  4. Agent startup, configuration, instance-role permission and endpoint connectivity
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: Agent startup, configuration, instance-role permission and endpoint connectivity

Clue. The missing signal is a guest metric, although built-in monitoring works.

  • Assume ASG reinstalls and starts every agent automatically: ASG launches the image; it does not independently guarantee arbitrary guest software startup.
  • Enable detailed monitoring to create the missing memory metric: Detailed EC2 monitoring changes built-in frequency, not guest memory collection.
  • Use the original image-source host’s metrics as proof: The new member needs its own correctly dimensioned telemetry.
  • Agent startup, configuration, instance-role permission and endpoint connectivity: The image supplies software; each running instance must actually start and publish the configured telemetry.

Change the requirement. If only built-in EC2 frequency is required, detailed monitoring can be the relevant choice.

Analogy. Packing a measuring tool in the box does not turn it on after delivery.

Images & deployment operations · CloudWatch metrics & alarms

2.1 · Desired versus actual

An ASG has actual capacity 3, desired 5 and maximum 10. A ChangeInCapacity policy adds 3. What desired capacity does it request?

  1. 6
  2. 8
  3. 10
  4. 3
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: 8

Clue. Policies change desired capacity, not actual capacity directly.

  • 6: Adds to actual rather than desired.
  • 8: The adjustment applies to desired 5; actual is then reconciled toward 8.
  • 10: The maximum is a cap, not the requested target.
  • 3: Ignores the scaling adjustment.

Change the requirement. If maximum were 6, the resulting desired capacity would be capped at 6.

Analogy. The staffing target changes before the new staff arrive.

Auto Scaling & elasticity

2.1 · Cache under write load

A node-based Redis OSS cluster has one busy primary and several replicas. Write throughput is the bottleneck. What change can distribute key writes when the key distribution supports it?

  1. Add replicas only
  2. Enable suitable cluster-mode sharding and distribute keys
  3. Increase CloudFront TTL
  4. Increase TTL only
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: Enable suitable cluster-mode sharding and distribute keys

Clue. Horizontal write scaling needs multiple shards, not more copies of one shard.

  • Add replicas only: Replicas copy a shard; they do not partition its primary writes.
  • Enable suitable cluster-mode sharding and distribute keys: Multiple primaries own different key ranges.
  • Increase CloudFront TTL: Does not directly repartition Redis writes.
  • Increase TTL only: Changes entry lifetime and potential read misses, not the number of write-owning shards.

Change the requirement. If reads dominated and stale reads were acceptable, replicas could improve read capacity.

Analogy. More photocopies do not create more editors; separate sections can have separate editors.

ElastiCache & cache operations

2.2 · Direct works, ALB fails

An instance answers on port 8080 directly, but ALB marks it unhealthy. Which investigation is most useful first?

  1. Health path/port/matcher and ALB-to-target SG rules
  2. Increase ASG desired capacity before checking the health configuration
  3. Disable all health checks
  4. Enable only EC2 status checks in the ASG
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: Health path/port/matcher and ALB-to-target SG rules

Clue. Direct reachability is not proof that the configured ALB check passes.

  • Health path/port/matcher and ALB-to-target SG rules: The load balancer uses its own configured request and source security boundary.
  • Increase ASG desired capacity before checking the health configuration: New instances with the same mismatched health setup can fail identically.
  • Disable all health checks: Hides evidence and risks routing to failures.
  • Enable only EC2 status checks in the ASG: Does not diagnose or repair the ALB application health-check request.

Change the requirement. If every target failed due to a bad application release, roll back the release rather than only changing checks.

Analogy. A front entrance working does not prove the inspector’s assigned entrance opens.

Load balancing & target health

2.2 · Standby or reader

A traditional RDS Multi-AZ DB instance must survive an AZ failure; separate reporting also needs read scaling with acceptable lag. Select TWO appropriate capabilities.

  1. Keep Multi-AZ for failover
  2. Add a suitable read replica and route reporting reads to it
  3. Read directly from the traditional standby
  4. Keep all reporting on the primary and expect automatic replica routing
  5. Treat a manual snapshot as automatic live database failover
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: Keep Multi-AZ for failover; Add a suitable read replica and route reporting reads to it

Clue. Availability and read scaling are separate requirements.

  • Keep Multi-AZ for failover: The synchronous standby supports availability.
  • Add a suitable read replica and route reporting reads to it: Adds asynchronous read capacity with lag considerations.
  • Read directly from the traditional standby: It is not a readable replica endpoint.
  • Keep all reporting on the primary and expect automatic replica routing: Applications must use the appropriate read endpoint; creating capacity alone does not redirect queries.
  • Treat a manual snapshot as automatic live database failover: Snapshots support recovery; they are not a running synchronous failover target.

Change the requirement. A Multi-AZ DB cluster or Aurora has a different readable-instance architecture; inspect the specified deployment model.

Analogy. Keep an emergency replacement and a separate reporting desk.

RDS, Aurora & database recovery

2.3 · Logical deletion

A valid table was deleted at 10:12; the RDS service is healthy and the standby has the deletion. PITR is enabled and 10:11 is within the recovery window. What is appropriate?

  1. Fail over to the standby
  2. Restore to a new DB at 10:11, validate and plan cutover
  3. Restart the current DB
  4. Restore only a snapshot taken after the 10:12 deletion
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: Restore to a new DB at 10:11, validate and plan cutover

Clue. Recover the state before the logical error, not merely a healthy host.

  • Fail over to the standby: The logical deletion has already replicated.
  • Restore to a new DB at 10:11, validate and plan cutover: Recovers historical state while preserving the source for investigation.
  • Restart the current DB: Does not undo committed deletion.
  • Restore only a snapshot taken after the 10:12 deletion: A post-deletion recovery point retains the unwanted logical state.

Change the requirement. For a host failure without logical corruption, managed failover is usually the relevant mechanism.

Analogy. A spare ledger with the same erasure cannot recover yesterday’s entry.

RDS, Aurora & database recovery · AWS Backup & disaster recovery

2.3 · Prove the recovery objective

A backup job is green. The runbook promises recovery in one hour with no more than fifteen minutes of lost data. Select TWO necessary validations.

  1. Time full restore, dependency setup and application cutover
  2. Check the latest usable recovery point against the incident time
  3. Assume green backup means both objectives are met
  4. Time only the restore API request being accepted
  5. Verify only that a backup plan exists
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: Time full restore, dependency setup and application cutover; Check the latest usable recovery point against the incident time

Clue. Both elapsed outage and recoverable data age need evidence.

  • Time full restore, dependency setup and application cutover: RTO covers usable recovery, not only API acceptance.
  • Check the latest usable recovery point against the incident time: Tests whether data loss can meet RPO.
  • Assume green backup means both objectives are met: A backup success does not test restoration.
  • Time only the restore API request being accepted: Acceptance excludes resource readiness, dependency configuration and usable application cutover.
  • Verify only that a backup plan exists: A configured plan does not prove backup job success or a working restore.

Change the requirement. If only retention compliance were asked, recovery-point retention and vault controls would be central.

Analogy. A packed parachute is not the same as a demonstrated safe landing.

AWS Backup & disaster recovery

2.3 · Version recovery

An object was overwritten yesterday in an S3 bucket that already had versioning enabled. The previous version is retained. What is the narrowest recovery?

  1. Retrieve the retained prior version and verify it before restoring the current object
  2. Fail over the RDS database
  3. Enable versioning now and assume it recreates yesterday’s data
  4. Delete the whole bucket
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: Retrieve the retained prior version and verify it before restoring the current object

Clue. The required historical object version already exists.

  • Retrieve the retained prior version and verify it before restoring the current object: Uses existing object history and avoids broad workload changes.
  • Fail over the RDS database: Unrelated to the overwritten S3 object.
  • Enable versioning now and assume it recreates yesterday’s data: Cannot retroactively create versions that were not retained.
  • Delete the whole bucket: Destroys unrelated data and is unnecessary.

Change the requirement. If versioning was not enabled and no other recovery copy existed, enabling it now could not recover the previous content.

Analogy. Use the earlier filing revision rather than replacing the entire office.

S3 operations & protection · AWS Backup & disaster recovery

2.3 · Deregistered image with retained recovery

An eligible EBS-backed AMI was accidentally deregistered. A matching Recycle Bin rule already covered it and retention has not expired. What should be checked first?

  1. Restore it through the applicable Recycle Bin recovery
  2. Assume every deregistration is immediately unrecoverable
  3. Create a rule now and expect it to protect past unretained deletions
  4. Assume deregistration already terminated its running instances
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: Restore it through the applicable Recycle Bin recovery

Clue. The rule existed before deletion and the retained item is still recoverable.

  • Restore it through the applicable Recycle Bin recovery: Preconfigured retention can preserve a deregistered eligible image.
  • Assume every deregistration is immediately unrecoverable: That ignores the specified retention mechanism.
  • Create a rule now and expect it to protect past unretained deletions: Retention rules are not retroactive recovery of data that was not retained.
  • Assume deregistration already terminated its running instances: Deregistration does not itself terminate instances previously launched from the image.

Change the requirement. Without applicable retention, investigate surviving snapshots/instances and reconstruct suitable image metadata if possible.

Analogy. A pre-arranged recovery bin can hold the discarded plan; adding a bin afterwards cannot recreate an already lost plan.

Images & deployment operations · AWS Backup & disaster recovery

2.3 · Durable image, unproven application state

A database application is captured in an EBS-backed AMI. The requirement is application-consistent recovery. Which statement is accurate?

  1. Coordinate application consistency and test recovery; allowing reboot helps flush buffered state
  2. Selecting No reboot always guarantees application consistency
  3. Provision more IOPS to make an inconsistent image transactionally valid
  4. Disable No reboot means prevent any reboot
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: Coordinate application consistency and test recovery; allowing reboot helps flush buffered state

Clue. Consistency is about a coherent application state, not simply retained bytes.

  • Coordinate application consistency and test recovery; allowing reboot helps flush buffered state: Durable captured blocks and a valid boot do not by themselves prove a coherent application transaction state.
  • Selecting No reboot always guarantees application consistency: Skipping quiescing/reboot can preserve inconsistent in-memory versus disk state.
  • Provision more IOPS to make an inconsistent image transactionally valid: I/O performance cannot reconstruct an uncoordinated application state.
  • Disable No reboot means prevent any reboot: It means clearing that option and allowing reboot, not prohibiting it.

Change the requirement. For an already stopped/quiesced application with validated procedures, capture requirements may differ.

Analogy. A photograph of durable ledger pages is useful only if the pages describe a consistent point in the transaction.

Images & deployment operations · AWS Backup & disaster recovery

2.3 · New disk must avoid first-read lazy loading

A supported restored EBS workload must be fully initialised at volume creation. Which preparation directly addresses that requirement?

  1. Enable FSR for the snapshot in the destination AZ, wait ready and check creation credits before creating the volume
  2. Increase provisioned IOPS alone
  3. Enable FSR only after creating the affected volume
  4. Enable FSR in an unrelated AZ because snapshots are Regional
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: Enable FSR for the snapshot in the destination AZ, wait ready and check creation credits before creating the volume

Clue. Immediate initialisation and steady-state I/O provisioning are separate mechanisms.

  • Enable FSR for the snapshot in the destination AZ, wait ready and check creation credits before creating the volume: FSR applies to the relevant snapshot/AZ and eligible new-volume creation.
  • Increase provisioned IOPS alone: Configured I/O capacity does not load missing snapshot blocks.
  • Enable FSR only after creating the affected volume: It does not retroactively convert that already-created volume into an FSR creation.
  • Enable FSR in an unrelated AZ because snapshots are Regional: The FSR preparation is destination-AZ specific despite the snapshot’s Regional scope.

Change the requirement. If a bounded initialisation interval is acceptable, evaluate current provisioned-initialisation-rate or manual-initialisation options.

Analogy. A faster disk motor does not pre-fill the restored pages before the first read.

EBS performance & snapshots

2.2 · All unhealthy does not mean guaranteed 503

All registered targets in an ALB target group are unhealthy. Which statement best describes the relevant distinction?

  1. ALB can fail open and route to unhealthy targets; actual HTTP results still depend on the request/target
  2. Every request must receive an ALB-generated 503 solely because health is Unhealthy
  3. ALB runs a fresh health check before every user request
  4. ASG must restart the failed application process instead of replacing an instance
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: ALB can fail open and route to unhealthy targets; actual HTTP results still depend on the request/target

Clue. Distinguish target health, routing behaviour and the origin of an HTTP status.

  • ALB can fail open and route to unhealthy targets; actual HTTP results still depend on the request/target: Health state is not a universal HTTP status mapping.
  • Every request must receive an ALB-generated 503 solely because health is Unhealthy: That confuses all-unhealthy fail-open with conditions such as no registered/all-unused targets.
  • ALB runs a fresh health check before every user request: Target health is evaluated periodically.
  • ASG must restart the failed application process instead of replacing an instance: ASG instance replacement and application restart are different mechanisms.

Change the requirement. With healthy B available and cross-zone routing applicable, ALB normally avoids unhealthy A rather than needing all-unhealthy fail-open.

Analogy. A dispatcher choosing among bad destinations cannot guarantee what status their doors will return.

Load balancing & target health · Auto Scaling & elasticity

2.1 · Repeated cache misses overload an origin

Several CloudFront cache locations repeatedly fetch the same uncached objects. The goal is to consolidate eligible origin-bound misses with managed CloudFront functionality. What fits?

  1. Origin Shield in a supported Region with low latency to the origin
  2. Weighted DNS alone
  3. Assume Origin Shield is a customer ElastiCache cluster
  4. Move the CloudFront distribution into the S3 bucket’s Region
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: Origin Shield in a supported Region with low latency to the origin

Clue. The missing mechanism is shared origin-miss consolidation, not merely more traffic destinations.

  • Origin Shield in a supported Region with low latency to the origin: Adds a managed caching/consolidation layer before the origin.
  • Weighted DNS alone: Distributes DNS answers without inherently consolidating identical origin fetches.
  • Assume Origin Shield is a customer ElastiCache cluster: It is part of CloudFront’s managed caching infrastructure.
  • Move the CloudFront distribution into the S3 bucket’s Region: A CloudFront distribution is global, not a Regional deployment to relocate.

Change the requirement. If values were custom application session data rather than HTTP object delivery, an application cache could be relevant.

Analogy. Several local counters can share one upstream copy desk instead of separately ordering the same item.

CloudFront & Global Accelerator · ElastiCache & cache operations

2.3 · Protection ends; deletion is separate

Compliance-mode Object Lock protected a version until yesterday. No legal hold remains and no Lifecycle expiration is configured. Must that version already be gone?

  1. No; retention expiry permits eligible deletion but does not schedule it
  2. Yes, Retain Until Date automatically deletes every version
  3. Lifecycle must delete it even while compliance retention is active
  4. A delete marker proves every retained version was destroyed
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: No; retention expiry permits eligible deletion but does not schedule it

Clue. Preservation and cleanup are separate controls.

  • No; retention expiry permits eligible deletion but does not schedule it: Automatic cleanup needs suitable version-aware Lifecycle rules or another authorised deletion action.
  • Yes, Retain Until Date automatically deletes every version: It is a protection deadline, not a deletion job.
  • Lifecycle must delete it even while compliance retention is active: Lifecycle cannot override active protection.
  • A delete marker proves every retained version was destroyed: A marker and the protected historical versions are distinct objects/states.

Change the requirement. If suitable Lifecycle rules were configured, eligible expiration can occur asynchronously after applicable protection ends.

Analogy. A contract saying “do not shred before Friday” does not itself order shredding on Friday.

S3 operations & protection · AWS Backup & disaster recovery

2.1 · Desired fell but four members remain

An ASG has four healthy in-service members, all protected from scale-in. A valid scale-in changes desired capacity from 4 to 3. What can happen?

  1. Desired becomes 3 while actual remains 4 until protection permits removal
  2. Desired must remain 4 because protection freezes it
  3. ASG must terminate an arbitrary protected member immediately
  4. All protected members become immune to health replacement
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: Desired becomes 3 while actual remains 4 until protection permits removal

Clue. All members are protected from the particular termination path.

  • Desired becomes 3 while actual remains 4 until protection permits removal: Desired is a target; protection can prevent convergence without preventing that target update.
  • Desired must remain 4 because protection freezes it: Protection controls eligible instance termination, not every desired-capacity change.
  • ASG must terminate an arbitrary protected member immediately: The assumed scale-in protection blocks selecting the protected members for ordinary scale-in.
  • All protected members become immune to health replacement: Scale-in protection does not prevent unhealthy replacement.

Change the requirement. If a member becomes unhealthy, replacement is a different operation.

Analogy. Changing the seat target does not evict a protected occupant.

Auto Scaling & elasticity

2.2 · Protected from API termination, then shutdown

DisableApiTermination is true. An EBS-root ASG member has InstanceInitiatedShutdownBehavior=terminate. Its administrator runs an OS shutdown. Which statement is correct?

  1. Scale-in protection prevents every unhealthy replacement
  2. Any AWS service can therefore ignore every protection
  3. OS shutdown can terminate it; ASG can restore desired capacity
  4. EC2 API protection must prevent OS shutdown
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: OS shutdown can terminate it; ASG can restore desired capacity

Clue. The question explicitly supplies the OS terminate setting.

  • Scale-in protection prevents every unhealthy replacement: The health-replacement path is not ordinary scale-in protection.
  • Any AWS service can therefore ignore every protection: The documented exceptions do not establish a universal rule for all services or controls.
  • OS shutdown can terminate it; ASG can restore desired capacity: API termination protection does not block the specified OS-initiated termination path.
  • EC2 API protection must prevent OS shutdown: The OS shutdown behaviour is separate from direct TerminateInstances protection.

Change the requirement. With shutdown behaviour stop, it stops first; ASG can subsequently replace the stopped member.

Analogy. A lock on the front-door API is not the switch on the machine itself.

EC2 performance & capacity · Auto Scaling & elasticity

2.3 · Restore into AZ B at full initial performance

A completed Regional snapshot originated from AZ A. New volumes must be created in AZ B with eligible full initial performance. What prepares the restore?

  1. Enable FSR for that snapshot in AZ B and wait for readiness plus sufficient credits
  2. Enable FSR only in source AZ A
  3. Increase IOPS and assume all snapshot blocks are already initialised
  4. Enable FSR after creating the affected volume to retroactively initialise it
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: Enable FSR for that snapshot in AZ B and wait for readiness plus sufficient credits

Clue. The deciding location is where the new volume is created.

  • Enable FSR for that snapshot in AZ B and wait for readiness plus sufficient credits: FSR is configured for the destination snapshot/AZ pair before creating the volume.
  • Enable FSR only in source AZ A: The source volume’s location does not initialise a new volume in another destination AZ.
  • Increase IOPS and assume all snapshot blocks are already initialised: Provisioned performance and loading snapshot data are separate mechanisms.
  • Enable FSR after creating the affected volume to retroactively initialise it: The FSR benefit applies at qualifying new-volume creation, not retroactively to the existing volume.

Change the requirement. If initialisation delay is acceptable, ordinary restore or supported initialisation-rate options may be more economical.

Analogy. Prepare the receiving workshop, not just the workshop the backup came from.

EBS performance & snapshots

2.1 · Discount commitment does not assure a launch

A workload must launch matching EC2 capacity in AZ A during an upcoming operation. It already has a Compute Savings Plan. What is still required for capacity assurance?

  1. Assume a Regional RI reserves capacity in every AZ
  2. Treat Savings Plan commitment as a maximum charge
  3. A suitable active AZ Capacity Reservation or matching Zonal RI
  4. Only increase ASG desired capacity
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: A suitable active AZ Capacity Reservation or matching Zonal RI

Clue. The requirement is availability of matching AZ capacity, beyond pricing.

  • Assume a Regional RI reserves capacity in every AZ: Regional RIs provide eligible discounts, not the Zonal capacity reservation.
  • Treat Savings Plan commitment as a maximum charge: Unused commitment still costs money; eligible uncovered excess is billed separately.
  • A suitable active AZ Capacity Reservation or matching Zonal RI: The billing commitment does not independently hold capacity in the required AZ.
  • Only increase ASG desired capacity: Desired is a requested target, not a reservation of available EC2 capacity.

Change the requirement. Cost flexibility without a launch-capacity requirement may favour an appropriate Savings Plan alone.

Analogy. A discount voucher is not a reserved seat.

EC2 performance & capacity · Auto Scaling & elasticity

2.3 · Offline import followed by archive storage

An eligible existing Snowball Edge customer imports local data and later archives eligible objects in an S3 Glacier class. What is the correct order?

  1. All new customers can order Snowball Edge without restrictions
  2. Local copy → return device → AWS imports into S3 → configured Lifecycle transition
  3. Snowball writes straight into Glacier without an S3 import
  4. A shipped device proves S3 objects are already available
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: Local copy → return device → AWS imports into S3 → configured Lifecycle transition

Clue. The customer is eligible, but import and archive transition are distinct stages.

  • All new customers can order Snowball Edge without restrictions: Current availability is limited to existing customers; older exam onboarding assumptions need a caveat.
  • Local copy → return device → AWS imports into S3 → configured Lifecycle transition: Physical transfer/import precedes the separate object storage-class transition.
  • Snowball writes straight into Glacier without an S3 import: The illustrated import lands in S3; the later Lifecycle action chooses the archive class.
  • A shipped device proves S3 objects are already available: Data still must be copied, returned and successfully imported.

Change the requirement. For a new customer, evaluate currently available online or physical-transfer alternatives.

Analogy. The courier delivery arrives before the warehouse files it in long-term storage.

S3 operations & protection

3.1 · Failed rollback

A stack is UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED because a required permission was removed. What should the operator do after restoring that permission?

  1. Run continue-update-rollback and verify final status
  2. Create another change set and assume it executes
  3. Delete the production stack immediately
  4. Edit only local CDK code without deploying
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: Run continue-update-rollback and verify final status

Clue. Rollback itself failed; repair it before another update.

  • Run continue-update-rollback and verify final status: Resumes the failed rollback using repaired prerequisites.
  • Create another change set and assume it executes: A preview does not resolve a stuck rollback.
  • Delete the production stack immediately: Destructive and not required by this failure.
  • Edit only local CDK code without deploying: Does not alter the current stack operation.

Change the requirement. For UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE you can plan a corrected new update after inspection.

Analogy. Repair the exit route before trying to finish reversing the truck.

CloudFormation & CDK lifecycle

3.1 · Drift is not repair

An operator manually changes a resource setting managed by a CloudFormation stack. What does drift detection do for supported tracked properties?

  1. Identifies supported differences against the stack definition
  2. Repairs every possible property automatically
  3. Treat NOT_CHECKED resources as confirmed IN_SYNC
  4. Rewrites the template to match reality
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: Identifies supported differences against the stack definition

Clue. Detection and remediation are separate operations.

  • Identifies supported differences against the stack definition: Detection reports differences; it is not automatic reconciliation.
  • Repairs every possible property automatically: Neither universal coverage nor automatic repair is guaranteed.
  • Treat NOT_CHECKED resources as confirmed IN_SYNC: Unsupported or unchecked resources have not been proven free of drift.
  • Rewrites the template to match reality: Not an automatic drift-detection effect.

Change the requirement. A deliberately updated template and executed change set could adopt a reviewed intended change.

Analogy. An inspection marks the deviation; it does not rebuild the wall.

CloudFormation & CDK lifecycle

3.1 · Share versus deploy

The organisation wants to deploy the same baseline stack in several accounts/Regions, and separately share an existing supported subnet. Select TWO correct tools.

  1. StackSets for baseline stack instances
  2. RAM for the supported existing subnet share
  3. Use RAM to deploy independent baseline stacks
  4. Use an SCP to create the required baseline resources
  5. Assume stack deployment automatically shares every created resource
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: StackSets for baseline stack instances; RAM for the supported existing subnet share

Clue. Deploy copies and share one resource are distinct responsibilities.

  • StackSets for baseline stack instances: Deploys and manages copies with execution controls.
  • RAM for the supported existing subnet share: Shares supported resources without recreating them.
  • Use RAM to deploy independent baseline stacks: RAM shares supported resources; it is not the stack-copy deployment mechanism.
  • Use an SCP to create the required baseline resources: SCPs restrict applicable operations; they do not provision the resources.
  • Assume stack deployment automatically shares every created resource: Cross-account sharing requires an appropriate supported sharing configuration.

Change the requirement. For one account/Region only, a normal CloudFormation stack may suffice.

Analogy. Print copies of the plan with StackSets; grant access to one existing room with RAM.

Multi-account operations · CloudFormation & CDK lifecycle

3.1 · Container rollout failure

Every new ECS task stops with an image-pull permission error; old tasks remain healthy. What should be examined first?

  1. Task execution-role registry permissions and image path/connectivity
  2. Only the application business-role SQL permissions
  3. Increase task CPU and memory as the permission fix
  4. Change the application runtime command before fixing the image pull
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: Task execution-role registry permissions and image path/connectivity

Clue. The failure happens before application execution.

  • Task execution-role registry permissions and image path/connectivity: These govern pulling the image; inspect events for the exact failure.
  • Only the application business-role SQL permissions: These apply after startup and do not explain the pull error.
  • Increase task CPU and memory as the permission fix: Resources cannot compensate for a denied image-pull operation.
  • Change the application runtime command before fixing the image pull: The application command is not reached when its image cannot be pulled.

Change the requirement. If the image pulled but the app failed to query DynamoDB, investigate the task role and app configuration.

Analogy. The installer cannot fetch the kit; debugging the installed program is premature.

Images & deployment operations

3.2 · Managed node offline

A private EC2 instance has SSM Agent installed but appears offline. No inbound SSH is allowed. Select TWO relevant checks.

  1. Instance profile and required Systems Manager permissions
  2. Outbound HTTPS/DNS access to required service endpoints
  3. Open inbound SSH to the world
  4. Permit only inbound HTTPS on the instance SG
  5. Restart the application process without checking agent identity or network
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: Instance profile and required Systems Manager permissions; Outbound HTTPS/DNS access to required service endpoints

Clue. Agent, identity and outbound network path are prerequisites.

  • Instance profile and required Systems Manager permissions: The agent needs an authorised identity.
  • Outbound HTTPS/DNS access to required service endpoints: The agent initiates service connectivity.
  • Open inbound SSH to the world: Not required for Systems Manager connectivity.
  • Permit only inbound HTTPS on the instance SG: The agent needs outbound service access; opening an inbound port does not supply it.
  • Restart the application process without checking agent identity or network: Does not repair the agent prerequisites that determine management connectivity.

Change the requirement. For a running Automation failing an EC2 API step, inspect the automation role rather than only node connectivity.

Analogy. A remote technician needs both an access card and a phone line.

Systems Manager operations · Endpoints & private connectivity

3.2 · Bounded operational repair

A recurring repair needs approval, several AWS API steps, concurrency limits and execution history. What is the best starting capability?

  1. Systems Manager Automation runbook
  2. An untracked SSH command on every instance
  3. Only an SNS topic
  4. A CloudWatch dashboard
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: Systems Manager Automation runbook

Clue. Repeatable governed maintenance is the requirement.

  • Systems Manager Automation runbook: Coordinates operational steps with approvals and controls.
  • An untracked SSH command on every instance: Lacks the stated coordinated controls.
  • Only an SNS topic: Notifies but does not perform the multi-step procedure.
  • A CloudWatch dashboard: Visualises evidence without executing the repair.

Change the requirement. For a simple stateless custom transformation, Lambda may be sufficient; EventBridge can trigger either.

Analogy. Use the controlled repair checklist rather than a broadcast message.

Systems Manager operations · EventBridge, SNS & remediation

3.1 · Repeatable AMI rollout

A patched AMI has passed tests. New ASG instances must use it, and existing instances must be replaced in controlled batches. Select TWO actions.

  1. Publish/select an appropriate launch-template version containing the AMI
  2. Run a configured instance refresh with health/warm-up controls
  3. Only change a tag on the old instances
  4. Assume copying an AMI updates running instances
  5. Delete all targets before checking healthy capacity
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: Publish/select an appropriate launch-template version containing the AMI; Run a configured instance refresh with health/warm-up controls

Clue. Artifact selection for new launches and replacement of existing instances are separate steps.

  • Publish/select an appropriate launch-template version containing the AMI: Defines the artifact used for subsequent launches.
  • Run a configured instance refresh with health/warm-up controls: Replaces existing instances gradually under the chosen deployment constraints.
  • Only change a tag on the old instances: Does not replace the running machine image.
  • Assume copying an AMI updates running instances: AMI creation/copying does not update already running instances.
  • Delete all targets before checking healthy capacity: Discards the requested controlled rollout and availability checks.

Change the requirement. If only future scale-out needed the AMI, updating the launch template could be sufficient without refreshing the current fleet.

Analogy. Update the installation kit, then schedule controlled replacements.

Images & deployment operations · Auto Scaling & elasticity

3.2 · Repair when the agent cannot run

An important EBS-backed instance has an impaired OS and no working SSM Agent connection. The approved goal is root-volume repair, not replacement. Which capability can fit?

  1. A suitable EC2Rescue Automation offline workflow with a temporary helper
  2. Repeat Run Command and assume it executes despite the missing agent path
  3. Assume installing the agent in the image proves it is now connected
  4. Replace it via ASG while expecting to retain the same repaired OS instance
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: A suitable EC2Rescue Automation offline workflow with a temporary helper

Clue. The target OS is unavailable, but the approved procedure can use external API-driven helper resources.

  • A suitable EC2Rescue Automation offline workflow with a temporary helper: Automation can orchestrate AWS APIs and offline disk inspection instead of relying on code inside the impaired OS.
  • Repeat Run Command and assume it executes despite the missing agent path: Ordinary agent-based commands still need a working managed-node connection.
  • Assume installing the agent in the image proves it is now connected: Installed software may be stopped or unable to reach its endpoints.
  • Replace it via ASG while expecting to retain the same repaired OS instance: Replacement and repairing this particular root disk are different outcomes.

Change the requirement. For disposable stateless ASG capacity, replacement may be preferable; do not accidentally mix it with an offline repair procedure.

Analogy. Repair the removed disk at a workshop rather than trying to run a command on a machine that cannot boot.

Systems Manager operations · EBS performance & snapshots

3.1 · Launch from an image is not disk transfer

An ASG launches another instance from an EBS-backed AMI. The original instance still uses its root volume. What normally happens?

  1. Fresh root volumes are created from the AMI’s referenced snapshots
  2. The original root disk is detached and moved to each new instance
  3. The Launch Template is itself the root disk snapshot
  4. The snapshot chooses instance type, SG and every launch setting automatically
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: Fresh root volumes are created from the AMI’s referenced snapshots

Clue. Image reference and new resource creation differ from reattaching an existing resource.

  • Fresh root volumes are created from the AMI’s referenced snapshots: The image describes boot metadata and captured disk state; the original working disk remains attached.
  • The original root disk is detached and moved to each new instance: That is not the normal image-based launch mechanism.
  • The Launch Template is itself the root disk snapshot: It supplies image and launch settings; it is not a disk backup.
  • The snapshot chooses instance type, SG and every launch setting automatically: Those launch choices are not all encoded by snapshot data alone.

Change the requirement. If explicitly recovering one existing data disk, a same-AZ detach/attach workflow is a different operation.

Analogy. A photocopied installation image creates another disk; it does not move the original disk.

Images & deployment operations · EBS performance & snapshots · Auto Scaling & elasticity

3.1 · Share for launch versus share for copy

Another account will launch an instance from a shared unencrypted AMI in the same Region. Must its backing snapshots always be shared separately for that launch?

  1. No; AMI sharing provides snapshot access needed for launch
  2. Yes, launching and copying always have identical permissions
  3. The AMI must always be copied merely to use another account
  4. The AMI is copied automatically to every AZ
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: No; AMI sharing provides snapshot access needed for launch

Clue. Name both the operation and changed boundary: launch, same Region, another account.

  • No; AMI sharing provides snapshot access needed for launch: Copying the shared image has different backing-storage permission requirements.
  • Yes, launching and copying always have identical permissions: This removes the documented distinction between the operations.
  • The AMI must always be copied merely to use another account: Same-Region cross-account launch permission can be sufficient in this unencrypted example.
  • The AMI is copied automatically to every AZ: An AMI is Regional; another AZ does not require a separate image copy.

Change the requirement. Encrypted sharing adds eligible KMS access; copying may additionally require storage read permissions.

Analogy. Permission to run the installation kit is not identical to permission to copy and redistribute it.

Images & deployment operations · KMS, encryption & secrets

3.1 · An allowed update must not replace the database

An operator may update a stack. A safeguard must reject accidental replacement of its existing database during updates while preserving ordinary stack administration. Which control fits?

  1. Stack termination protection alone
  2. DeletionPolicy: Retain alone
  3. Only grant broader IAM permissions
  4. A stack policy denying Update:Replace for that logical resource
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: A stack policy denying Update:Replace for that logical resource

Clue. The forbidden operation is replacement during a stack update.

  • Stack termination protection alone: Protects deletion of the whole stack, not every replacement during an update.
  • DeletionPolicy: Retain alone: Controls resource preservation at deletion/removal boundaries; it is not the requested update-action prohibition.
  • Only grant broader IAM permissions: More caller permissions cannot implement a guard against an unwanted protected update.
  • A stack policy denying Update:Replace for that logical resource: Stack policies restrict existing-resource update actions independently of the caller’s UpdateStack permission.

Change the requirement. If the requirement were to prevent deleting the entire stack, choose termination protection.

Analogy. Permission to renovate a building is separate from a rule protecting one room.

CloudFormation & CDK lifecycle · IAM access investigation

3.1 · The second Region reports AlreadyExists
