The same account deploys a template in Sydney and Melbourne. Both templates declare RoleName: shared-app. The second fails because the role exists. What is the clearest correction when each deployment needs its own role?

  1. Change the instance subnet
  2. Assume no resources were created because the stack failed
  3. Generate names or include Region/stack identity
  4. Retry until CloudFormation silently adopts it
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: Generate names or include Region/stack identity

Clue. A new create operation is colliding with an account-wide physical name.

  • Change the instance subnet: Subnet placement does not alter the IAM role’s account-wide namespace.
  • Assume no resources were created because the stack failed: Earlier successful creates can precede a later failure; inspect rollback and stack events.
  • Generate names or include Region/stack identity: IAM names are account-wide although the two owning stacks are Regional.
  • Retry until CloudFormation silently adopts it: Matching a name does not automatically import an existing resource into a different stack.

Change the requirement. For one intentionally shared role, keep a single owner and pass its ARN instead of creating it twice.

Analogy. Two regional construction teams cannot separately register the same account-wide name.

CloudFormation & CDK lifecycle · IAM access investigation

3.1 · One baseline across account–Region targets

An operations team must maintain the same approved template in two accounts and two Regions, controlling Region order and rollout concurrency. What fits?

  1. Share an AMI instead of deploying the baseline
  2. CloudFormation StackSets
  3. One ordinary stack becomes global
  4. Use unrelated templates as an arbitrary dependency graph in one StackSet
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: CloudFormation StackSets

Clue. The same template is repeated at explicit account–Region targets.

  • Share an AMI instead of deploying the baseline: An AMI supplies launch artifacts, not every resource in the infrastructure baseline.
  • CloudFormation StackSets: Creates and manages a distinct stack for each selected account–Region combination.
  • One ordinary stack becomes global: A normal stack is Regional and does not automatically span target accounts and Regions.
  • Use unrelated templates as an arbitrary dependency graph in one StackSet: A StackSet has a common template, not a general workflow for unrelated templates.

Change the requirement. Different templates with cross-workflow dependencies need a separate orchestration design.

Analogy. One blueprint produces separate buildings; it does not produce one building in four places.

Multi-account operations · CloudFormation & CDK lifecycle

3.1 · Encrypted image moves to another Region

One account needs to copy its EBS-backed AMI from Sydney to Melbourne. The source snapshots use aws/ebs. Which statement is accurate?

  1. Use the Sydney AMI ID directly in Melbourne
  2. An ordinary customer-managed key is global
  3. A same-account cross-Region copy can use an appropriate destination-Region key
  4. AWS-managed encryption prevents every AMI copy
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: A same-account cross-Region copy can use an appropriate destination-Region key

Clue. Account ownership stays the same; the Region changes.

  • Use the Sydney AMI ID directly in Melbourne: AMI IDs and their usable resources are Regional.
  • An ordinary customer-managed key is global: KMS keys are Regional; multi-Region keys still have Regional primary/replica resources.
  • A same-account cross-Region copy can use an appropriate destination-Region key: The cross-account restriction on sharing aws/ebs does not prohibit this same-account Region-copy workflow.
  • AWS-managed encryption prevents every AMI copy: That confuses cross-account key sharing with a separate cross-Region copy operation.

Change the requirement. Another account using the encrypted image also requires appropriate sharing and customer-managed key access.

Analogy. Moving a regional copy and lending another company your key are different operations.

Images & deployment operations · KMS, encryption & secrets

3.2 · Snapshots every five minutes

An existing EBS volume needs a recurring CreateSnapshot request every five minutes. No custom processing is required. Which modern configuration fits?

  1. DLM five-minute lifecycle schedule
  2. AWS Backup snapshot rule every five minutes
  3. Lambda function without a trigger
  4. EventBridge Scheduler rate(5 minutes) → authorised EC2 CreateSnapshot target
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: EventBridge Scheduler rate(5 minutes) → authorised EC2 CreateSnapshot target

Clue. The explicit sub-hour interval changes the otherwise useful managed-lifecycle answer.

  • DLM five-minute lifecycle schedule: DLM custom snapshot schedules have a one-hour minimum, not the requested five-minute interval.
  • AWS Backup snapshot rule every five minutes: Scheduled snapshot-backup rules have a minimum hourly frequency; continuous backup is a different supported-resource feature.
  • Lambda function without a trigger: Custom function code does not by itself define recurring execution.
  • EventBridge Scheduler rate(5 minutes) → authorised EC2 CreateSnapshot target: Scheduler can invoke the supported API directly; snapshot completion and retention remain separate concerns.

Change the requirement. Hourly EBS creation plus retention/deletion points to DLM; central multi-service protection points to AWS Backup.

Analogy. A recurring timer and a retention clerk perform different jobs.

EventBridge, SNS & remediation · EBS performance & snapshots · AWS Backup & disaster recovery

4.1 · Guardrail denial

A member-account role has an identity Allow for an operation, but an applicable SCP explicitly denies it. What happens?

  1. Denied
  2. Allowed because the role is trusted
  3. Allowed because SCPs grant permissions
  4. Allowed because a permissions-boundary Allow overrides the SCP Deny
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: Denied

Clue. An applicable explicit deny is decisive.

  • Denied: An applicable explicit deny overrides the allow.
  • Allowed because the role is trusted: Trust establishes assumption, not exemption from guardrails.
  • Allowed because SCPs grant permissions: SCPs limit available permissions; they do not grant an action to a role.
  • Allowed because a permissions-boundary Allow overrides the SCP Deny: A boundary is another limit; it cannot override an applicable explicit deny.

Change the requirement. If no limiting deny applied, evaluate the remaining applicable permissions and resource-policy conditions.

Analogy. A room pass does not override a building-wide prohibition.

IAM access investigation · Multi-account operations

4.1 · Continuous property checks

An operator must record configuration history and continuously evaluate approved resource settings across accounts. Select TWO needed elements.

  1. Appropriate Config recorders and rules in source accounts/Regions
  2. An aggregator for the central supported view
  3. Only an Artifact report
  4. Configure only an aggregator and disable source recorders
  5. Use CloudTrail alone to evaluate and enforce every resource property rule
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: Appropriate Config recorders and rules in source accounts/Regions; An aggregator for the central supported view

Clue. Central visibility depends on configured source evidence.

  • Appropriate Config recorders and rules in source accounts/Regions: Produce the history and evaluations.
  • An aggregator for the central supported view: Collects views but does not replace source recording.
  • Only an Artifact report: Reports AWS compliance evidence, not customer resource changes.
  • Configure only an aggregator and disable source recorders: The central view cannot substitute for the required recording/evaluation at sources.
  • Use CloudTrail alone to evaluate and enforce every resource property rule: API audit evidence is useful but is not Config configuration-rule evaluation.

Change the requirement. To identify which API actor changed a setting, add CloudTrail evidence.

Analogy. A central register needs inspections actually performed at each site.

Config & continuous compliance · CloudTrail & change evidence

4.2 · Encrypted object denied

A role can access a bucket, but GetObject fails for an SSE-KMS object using a customer-managed key. Select TWO relevant checks.

  1. Key policy/IAM/grants for kms:Decrypt
  2. Key state, Region and required encryption context
  3. Add another s3:GetObject Allow without checking key access
  4. Assume bucket permission always includes key use
  5. Enable key rotation and expect it to override the denied policy
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: Key policy/IAM/grants for kms:Decrypt; Key state, Region and required encryption context

Clue. The encrypted data and cryptographic key have separate controls.

  • Key policy/IAM/grants for kms:Decrypt: KMS authorisation is distinct from object access.
  • Key state, Region and required encryption context: Even otherwise allowed access can fail if the key or context is wrong.
  • Add another s3:GetObject Allow without checking key access: Repeating resource permission does not grant the missing cryptographic permission.
  • Assume bucket permission always includes key use: Incorrect separation of permissions.
  • Enable key rotation and expect it to override the denied policy: Rotation changes cryptographic material management, not authorisation decisions.

Change the requirement. For SSE-S3, customer KMS decrypt permission would not be the corresponding dependency.

Analogy. The cabinet pass and the key-use permission are separate.

KMS, encryption & secrets

4.2 · Find the right security source

A report lists a vulnerable package version on supported EC2 workloads. Which service most directly supplies this assessment?

  1. Inspector
  2. Macie
  3. GuardDuty
  4. Artifact
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: Inspector

Clue. Package vulnerability assessment, rather than data discovery or API auditing.

  • Inspector: Assesses supported workload software vulnerabilities/exposure.
  • Macie: Discovers sensitive S3 data.
  • GuardDuty: Investigates supported threat/activity signals rather than replacing Inspector package assessment.
  • Artifact: Provides AWS compliance documentation.

Change the requirement. Suspicious credential activity would point toward GuardDuty investigation.

Analogy. Use the mechanical inspection report for a faulty component, not a document classification report.

Security findings & classification

4.2 · Certificate placement

An ALB in ap-southeast-2 needs an ACM certificate for its HTTPS listener. A matching certificate exists only in us-east-1. What is required?

  1. Request/import a suitable certificate in ap-southeast-2 and attach it
  2. Attach the us-east-1 certificate directly because all ACM certificates are global
  3. Change the target group without obtaining a regional listener certificate
  4. Disable TLS permanently
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: Request/import a suitable certificate in ap-southeast-2 and attach it

Clue. Certificate Region is determined by the TLS termination service.

  • Request/import a suitable certificate in ap-southeast-2 and attach it: ALB certificate resources must be in its Region; verify domain validation and hostname coverage.
  • Attach the us-east-1 certificate directly because all ACM certificates are global: ACM certificates used by ALB are regional.
  • Change the target group without obtaining a regional listener certificate: Backend target selection does not satisfy the frontend certificate Region requirement.
  • Disable TLS permanently: Does not meet the HTTPS requirement.

Change the requirement. For a CloudFront viewer certificate, ACM in us-east-1 is the required special case.

Analogy. The right identity document must be available at the endpoint that presents it.

ACM & encrypted connections · Load balancing & target health

4.2 · Same-account encrypted ASG launch

An ASG cannot launch from an image encrypted under a customer-managed key in its own account. The application role has decrypt access. Which identity still needs the documented launch-time key permissions?

  1. The ASG service-linked role
  2. Only the application instance profile again
  3. A new cross-account AssumeRole session, despite same-account ownership
  4. Any IAM user with console sign-in but no key policy access
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: The ASG service-linked role

Clue. The failure precedes application startup; authorise the launch-time service identity.

  • The ASG service-linked role: It participates in provisioning the encrypted volumes before the application instance profile can run.
  • Only the application instance profile again: Runtime application permission does not authorise the launch workflow.
  • A new cross-account AssumeRole session, despite same-account ownership: No foreign account is specified; assumption is not the missing control in this question.
  • Any IAM user with console sign-in but no key policy access: Console authentication does not supply the required KMS authorisation.

Change the requirement. With an external key owner, use the documented cross-account key-policy and grant workflow.

Analogy. Give the installation crew permission to open the kit; the eventual resident’s key is a different permission.

KMS, encryption & secrets · Images & deployment operations · Auto Scaling & elasticity

4.2 · Cross-account key: grant, not role assumption

The ASG is in account A; its image’s snapshots use a customer-managed KMS key in account B. AMI access is valid. Which additional AWS-documented combination enables the ASG launch identity?

  1. Suitable key policy plus an explicit KMS grant to the ASG service-linked role
  2. Only AssumeRole into account B with no key grant
  3. Only add the app instance profile to an S3 bucket policy
  4. Copy and re-encrypt as the only possible solution
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: Suitable key policy plus an explicit KMS grant to the ASG service-linked role

Clue. The deciding fact is that key ownership differs from ASG ownership.

  • Suitable key policy plus an explicit KMS grant to the ASG service-linked role: The external key owner must authorise the documented cross-account grant path.
  • Only AssumeRole into account B with no key grant: Role assumption is not the prescribed ASG service-linked-role KMS grant mechanism.
  • Only add the app instance profile to an S3 bucket policy: That addresses neither the launch-time identity nor the encrypted EBS key.
  • Copy and re-encrypt as the only possible solution: That can be an alternative, but is not mandatory when supported key-policy/grant access is configured.

Change the requirement. For a same-account key, configure the service-linked role’s documented key policy instead of assuming foreign ownership.

Analogy. The other building can authorise a specific installation crew through a key grant without lending that crew an employee identity.

KMS, encryption & secrets · Images & deployment operations · Auto Scaling & elasticity

4.1 · Object access audit coverage and cost

A management-event trail exists. The team needs CloudTrail identity evidence for S3 GetObject operations. Which statement is accurate?

  1. Configure appropriate object data-event selectors and account for data-event charges
  2. Assume management event history already includes every GetObject
  3. Treat best-effort server access logs as a guaranteed immediate complete CloudTrail feed
  4. Assume no S3 server-log delivery fee means every logging destination and query is free
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: Configure appropriate object data-event selectors and account for data-event charges

Clue. Choose the evidence type and event coverage before assuming a trail satisfies the audit requirement.

  • Configure appropriate object data-event selectors and account for data-event charges: Management events alone do not provide the requested object-level coverage.
  • Assume management event history already includes every GetObject: Object data operations require their own applicable logging configuration.
  • Treat best-effort server access logs as a guaranteed immediate complete CloudTrail feed: Different delivery/completeness and identity-evidence semantics apply.
  • Assume no S3 server-log delivery fee means every logging destination and query is free: Storage/access/analysis cost remains, and other delivery destinations can have ingestion charges.

Change the requirement. For best-effort access analysis with logs delivered to S3, the service’s direct delivery fee model differs.

Analogy. A register of administrative changes does not automatically contain every document read.

S3 operations & protection · CloudTrail & change evidence

4.1 · Copy HR and Audit objects into Finance

A Finance identity can write its destination bucket. HR and Audit must permit that identity to copy selected source objects. Which approach keeps the permission path simplest?

  1. Grant only source GetObject because CopyObject needs no destination permission
  2. Grant Finance source GetObject in its identity policy and source bucket policies, keeping Finance credentials
  3. Assume an HR role and automatically inherit Finance write access
  4. Put a role trust policy on the S3 bucket
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: Grant Finance source GetObject in its identity policy and source bucket policies, keeping Finance credentials

Clue. The same effective principal must be allowed at both ends.

  • Grant only source GetObject because CopyObject needs no destination permission: The operation also requires the applicable destination PutObject permission.
  • Grant Finance source GetObject in its identity policy and source bucket policies, keeping Finance credentials: The same copy credentials can then satisfy both source reads and destination writes.
  • Assume an HR role and automatically inherit Finance write access: Assumed-role credentials do not union their permissions with the original user’s Finance permissions.
  • Put a role trust policy on the S3 bucket: S3 bucket policies grant resource access; an IAM role trust policy governs role assumption.

Change the requirement. A deliberately authorised source role could work if it also has the destination access; it is not automatic.

Analogy. Changing badges does not keep the doors your previous badge opened.

IAM access investigation · S3 operations & protection

5.1 · Private S3 route

Private EC2 instances in one VPC need same-Region S3 API access without NAT. What is usually the appropriate lowest-overhead endpoint?

  1. S3 gateway endpoint associated with relevant route tables
  2. Internet gateway alone with no addressing changes
  3. A DNS alias without any network path
  4. An S3 gateway endpoint security group
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: S3 gateway endpoint associated with relevant route tables

Clue. Same-VPC gateway endpoint use case, not remote on-premises access.

  • S3 gateway endpoint associated with relevant route tables: Provides a prefix-list route; IAM/bucket/KMS access still applies.
  • Internet gateway alone with no addressing changes: Does not give private-only IPv4 instances direct internet access.
  • A DNS alias without any network path: Names do not provide routing.
  • An S3 gateway endpoint security group: Gateway endpoints do not use interface ENI security groups.

Change the requirement. For supported remote/hybrid S3 access through private ENIs, consider an interface endpoint and its DNS/cost model.

Analogy. Choose the direct service road instead of buying an internet exit.

5.1 · Private egress cost

A zonal NAT gateway in AZ A carries large egress from workloads in AZ B. Which change should be evaluated against availability and cost requirements?

  1. AZ-aligned NAT paths and applicable service endpoints
  2. Assume every additional NAT is always cheaper
  3. Send arbitrary internet egress through an S3 gateway endpoint
  4. Choose interface endpoints for every service without comparing charges
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: AZ-aligned NAT paths and applicable service endpoints

Clue. Compare processing, cross-AZ transfer and availability together.

  • AZ-aligned NAT paths and applicable service endpoints: Can reduce cross-AZ dependency/transfer; compare added NAT hourly cost and endpoint charges.
  • Assume every additional NAT is always cheaper: Hourly and volume costs vary.
  • Send arbitrary internet egress through an S3 gateway endpoint: The endpoint routes supported S3 traffic; it is not a general internet egress service.
  • Choose interface endpoints for every service without comparing charges: Availability, service support, hourly cost, data processing and AZ traffic still need evaluation.

Change the requirement. At very low volume a central path may be cheaper if its resilience trade-off is accepted.

Analogy. A local exit avoids a cross-town trip, but another exit has its own upkeep cost.

VPC routes, subnets & filters · Endpoints & private connectivity

5.2 · Private-name resolution

An AWS instance resolves an internal private hosted-zone name, but on-premises clients cannot. What should be checked first?

  1. Resolver inbound endpoint, conditional forwarding and its network path
  2. Change only a public hosted-zone record for the private name
  3. Add only an AWS outbound Resolver endpoint for queries coming from on premises
  4. Lower the private record TTL without establishing forwarding
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: Resolver inbound endpoint, conditional forwarding and its network path

Clue. The failure is scoped to hybrid DNS clients.

  • Resolver inbound endpoint, conditional forwarding and its network path: Enables hybrid clients to query the appropriate AWS resolver path.
  • Change only a public hosted-zone record for the private name: Does not configure on-premises access to the intended private DNS view.
  • Add only an AWS outbound Resolver endpoint for queries coming from on premises: Inbound and outbound endpoint directions differ; remote queries need the appropriate inbound resolution path.
  • Lower the private record TTL without establishing forwarding: Changes cache time, not access to the resolver that can answer the private name.

Change the requirement. If DNS answered correctly but the TCP connection timed out, investigate routes/filters/target.

Analogy. The address exists in the branch directory but the head office cannot reach that directory.

Route 53 & DNS operations · Endpoints & private connectivity

5.2 · Incorrect cached language

CloudFront forwards lang to an origin that varies content by language, but its cache key ignores lang. Users receive another language. What fixes correctness?

  1. Include lang in the appropriate cache policy and address existing entries
  2. Lower TTL only
  3. Add lang only to the origin request policy, leaving the cache key unchanged
  4. Add an unrelated header to the cache key while still ignoring lang
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: Include lang in the appropriate cache policy and address existing entries

Clue. The cache treats different content variants as the same key.

  • Include lang in the appropriate cache policy and address existing entries: Separates response variants.
  • Lower TTL only: Shortens the wrong sharing interval without fixing the key.
  • Add lang only to the origin request policy, leaving the cache key unchanged: Forwarding a value does not necessarily partition cached responses by that value.
  • Add an unrelated header to the cache key while still ignoring lang: Does not distinguish the response dimension causing the incorrect language reuse.

Change the requirement. If the response never varied by language, excluding lang would improve reuse without harming correctness.

Analogy. Different editions need different shelf labels.

CloudFront & Global Accelerator

5.3 · Response-only block

For a browser connection browser:54321 → ALB:443, a stateless subnet NACL permits inbound 443 but blocks outbound destination 54321. What occurs?

  1. The response can be blocked; allow the relevant ephemeral return range
  2. The inbound rule automatically permits the return
  3. Change only the backend SG to repair the ALB subnet outbound NACL
  4. Outbound destination 443 alone fixes this browser response
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: The response can be blocked; allow the relevant ephemeral return range

Clue. Response destination differs from request destination.

  • The response can be blocked; allow the relevant ephemeral return range: NACLs independently evaluate both directions.
  • The inbound rule automatically permits the return: That describes stateful SG handling, not NACLs.
  • Change only the backend SG to repair the ALB subnet outbound NACL: A different security boundary cannot override this explicit return-path filter.
  • Outbound destination 443 alone fixes this browser response: The browser response destination is its ephemeral port.

Change the requirement. For a security group tracking the established allowed flow, return traffic is automatically permitted.

Analogy. A two-way trip needs the return gate open too.

VPC routes, subnets & filters · Network evidence & protection

5.3 · Model versus live traffic

Reachability Analyzer reports a supported path reachable, but the application still times out. Select TWO useful next checks.

  1. Application listener, target health and OS firewall
  2. Actual flow/access logs and measured network/application outcome
  3. Conclude every packet must succeed
  4. Assume a correct DNS answer proves the application is healthy
  5. Treat Flow Logs ACCEPT as business success
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: Application listener, target health and OS firewall; Actual flow/access logs and measured network/application outcome

Clue. A configuration model and a live application test prove different things.

  • Application listener, target health and OS firewall: Configuration modelling does not prove the process is accepting traffic.
  • Actual flow/access logs and measured network/application outcome: Tests real requests at the relevant time and source.
  • Conclude every packet must succeed: Modelled reachability is not a live traffic guarantee.
  • Assume a correct DNS answer proves the application is healthy: Name resolution does not prove the target process is listening or responding.
  • Treat Flow Logs ACCEPT as business success: Acceptance is not an application result.

Change the requirement. If the model identified a blocking route, correct that proven dependency before application tuning.

Analogy. A clear road map does not prove the shop is open.

Network evidence & protection · Load balancing & target health

5.3 · Same VPC, different subnet, SQL timeout

An EC2 app and RDS MySQL instance use different subnets in one VPC. Local routes are intact, NACLs permit both directions, DNS is correct and MySQL is listening. The DB SG has no app ingress. What fixes the first proven block?

  1. Allow the database port from the app SG in the DB SG
  2. Create VPC peering between the two subnets
  3. Add a NAT gateway to the database subnet
  4. Grant the app role AdministratorAccess
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: Allow the database port from the app SG in the DB SG

Clue. Evidence already establishes routing; the missing control is database ingress.

  • Allow the database port from the app SG in the DB SG: The routing path exists; resource-level ingress is missing.
  • Create VPC peering between the two subnets: Peering joins VPCs, not subnets already sharing the VPC local path.
  • Add a NAT gateway to the database subnet: NAT is not required for this same-VPC private database connection.
  • Grant the app role AdministratorAccess: IAM permissions do not open the database’s network security group.

Change the requirement. If the route were blackholed by a deliberate routing change, fix the proven path first.

Analogy. The road reaches the building, but its gate still needs to admit the visitor.

VPC routes, subnets & filters · RDS, Aurora & database recovery

5.1 · Custom NACL starts closed

A routed app-to-DB path uses a newly created custom NACL with no allow rules and a new DB SG with no inbound rules. Which TWO configurations are needed for the assumed TCP path?

  1. DB SG ingress on the database port from the app SG
  2. Custom NACL rules for the request and relevant return traffic
  3. Rely on the default NACL allow rules in this custom NACL
  4. Assume the default SG self-reference opens every new SG
  5. Enable an egress-only IGW for private IPv4 SQL
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: DB SG ingress on the database port from the app SG; Custom NACL rules for the request and relevant return traffic

Clue. Name the exact initial control type: custom NACL and custom SG.

  • DB SG ingress on the database port from the app SG: New custom SGs do not start with arbitrary inbound access.
  • Custom NACL rules for the request and relevant return traffic: A custom NACL initially denies and is stateless.
  • Rely on the default NACL allow rules in this custom NACL: A newly created custom NACL does not inherit the default NACL’s allow-all rules.
  • Assume the default SG self-reference opens every new SG: That self-reference applies to the default SG’s members, not every group.
  • Enable an egress-only IGW for private IPv4 SQL: An egress-only IGW is IPv6 internet egress, not this local SQL path.

Change the requirement. With an unchanged default NACL, its initial allow rules would remove that particular NACL block; DB SG ingress could still be needed.

Analogy. A new checkpoint can start shut even though the site’s original checkpoint started open.

VPC routes, subnets & filters

5.1 · Public route but no public IPv4

A subnet routes 0.0.0.0/0 to an IGW, but an instance has only private IPv4. Filters are valid. What is still needed for direct IPv4 internet access?

  1. Suitable public IPv4/EIP addressing on the instance
  2. Only a larger instance type
  3. An egress-only IGW for its private IPv4
  4. A different subnet name
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: Suitable public IPv4/EIP addressing on the instance

Clue. Direct IPv4 access requires both the path and suitable public addressing.

  • Suitable public IPv4/EIP addressing on the instance: The IGW route alone does not supply a direct public IPv4 identity.
  • Only a larger instance type: CPU and memory do not supply missing public addressing.
  • An egress-only IGW for its private IPv4: That gateway supports IPv6, not direct IPv4 connectivity.
  • A different subnet name: Names do not change addressing, routes or traffic controls.

Change the requirement. If the instance must remain private, use an appropriate NAT/endpoint path instead of direct public addressing.

Analogy. An exit road does not automatically give the vehicle a public return address.

VPC routes, subnets & filters

5.1 · IPv6 outbound only

Instances with deliberately assigned IPv6 addresses need outbound internet connections and replies, with no new inbound internet connections. Which gateway fits?

  1. Egress-only internet gateway with the IPv6 route and controls
  2. Public NAT gateway as if it were an IPv6 egress-only IGW
  3. Only an IPv4 route to an IGW
  4. No configuration because every EC2 instance automatically has IPv6
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: Egress-only internet gateway with the IPv6 route and controls

Clue. The protocol and initiation direction jointly decide the gateway.

  • Egress-only internet gateway with the IPv6 route and controls: Designed for outbound-initiated IPv6 internet communication.
  • Public NAT gateway as if it were an IPv6 egress-only IGW: Private IPv4 NAT egress and native IPv6 outbound-only routing are different mechanisms.
  • Only an IPv4 route to an IGW: An IPv4 route does not route the separate IPv6 address space.
  • No configuration because every EC2 instance automatically has IPv6: IPv6 CIDR/address assignment and routing are not automatic for every instance.

Change the requirement. For private IPv4 outbound internet traffic, a suitable NAT path would be relevant.

Analogy. Choose the gate for the address family printed on the vehicle’s address.

VPC routes, subnets & filters

5.2 · Private origin and website endpoint

A distribution uses an S3 website endpoint. The requirement is authenticated CloudFront-only S3 access using OAC. Which change fits?

  1. Use the S3 REST origin with appropriate OAC and a scoped bucket policy
  2. Attach OAC directly to the website endpoint
  3. Add HTTPS to the S3 website endpoint URL and assume support
  4. Treat a secret Referer header as equivalent to OAC authentication
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: Use the S3 REST origin with appropriate OAC and a scoped bucket policy

Clue. The origin endpoint type determines the authentication and transport features available.

  • Use the S3 REST origin with appropriate OAC and a scoped bucket policy: OAC supports the REST-origin model; the website endpoint remains a custom HTTP origin.
  • Attach OAC directly to the website endpoint: OAC/OAI do not apply to the website custom-origin endpoint.
  • Add HTTPS to the S3 website endpoint URL and assume support: S3 website endpoints do not provide HTTPS themselves.
  • Treat a secret Referer header as equivalent to OAC authentication: A spoofable header condition is a limited workaround, not the same trust mechanism.

Change the requirement. When website behaviour is deliberately retained, evaluate its custom-origin limitations rather than claiming OAC support.

Analogy. A different sign above the website entrance does not turn it into the authenticated API entrance.

CloudFront & Global Accelerator · S3 operations & protection

5.3 · Explicit S3 wrong-signing-Region error

A bucket name was deleted and recreated in Singapore. CloudFront receives AuthorizationHeaderMalformed: signed for ap-southeast-2, expected ap-southeast-1. What should be corrected first?

  1. Refresh/update the origin’s current bucket information, deploy and verify the signing scope
  2. Assign a home Region to the access key
  3. Move the global CloudFront distribution to Singapore
  4. Only open a VPC SG because every authorisation error is a timeout
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: Refresh/update the origin’s current bucket information, deploy and verify the signing scope

Clue. Resource location and signature scope must agree; neither is a JSON-body routing field.

  • Refresh/update the origin’s current bucket information, deploy and verify the signing scope: The explicit response identifies stale origin/signing Region information.
  • Assign a home Region to the access key: Access keys do not carry that Regional ownership property.
  • Move the global CloudFront distribution to Singapore: A distribution is not a Regional resource to move.
  • Only open a VPC SG because every authorisation error is a timeout: S3 returned an explicit HTTP error; that is not evidence of a failed network connection.

Change the requirement. A timeout without an S3 response would require a different connectivity investigation.

Analogy. The parcel arrived, but the signed identity scope named the wrong regional authority.

CloudFront & Global Accelerator · S3 operations & protection

5.1 · Public destination does not select peering

Two EC2 workloads in ordinary AWS Regions use public IP addresses. A peering connection is then created, but requests still target those public IPs. Which statement is accurate?

  1. AWS documents AWS-to-AWS public-IP traffic staying on its network, and peering needs private destinations/routes
  2. Public addressing always proves external-internet transit
  3. Peering automatically redirects every public-IP call
  4. Direct Connect is automatically inserted
Answer & deciding boundary

Correct: AWS documents AWS-to-AWS public-IP traffic staying on its network, and peering needs private destinations/routes

Clue. Address selection and connectivity configuration have not changed.

  • AWS documents AWS-to-AWS public-IP traffic staying on its network, and peering needs private destinations/routes: Public addressing is separate from the physical AWS network path; peering does not rewrite those requests.
  • Public addressing always proves external-internet transit: Current AWS guidance contradicts that blanket statement; China/Sovereign Cloud exceptions are separately documented.
  • Peering automatically redirects every public-IP call: Peering routes private connectivity; merely creating it does not change public-IP destinations.
  • Direct Connect is automatically inserted: Direct Connect is a separately provisioned network connection, not an automatic EC2 communication hop.

Change the requirement. A private-address requirement needs suitable private routes/connectivity and permitted traffic.

Analogy. A public street address does not identify which owned road carried the delivery.

VPC routes, subnets & filters

CloudWatch metrics & alarms

Measure workload behaviour; alarm on a defined statistic, dimension and time window.

Flow. Resource / agent → metric → alarm evaluation → configured action → verified outcome.

  • EC2 basic monitoring usually publishes at five-minute intervals; detailed monitoring usually changes this to one minute. Memory and filesystem utilisation need an agent or custom publisher.
  • Standard-resolution custom metrics use one-minute resolution; high-resolution metrics can publish at one second. Pick a supported alarm period and statistic; percentile latency and average latency answer different questions. Select the metric’s storage resolution when publishing with PutMetricData.
  • M out of N means at least M breaching datapoints among N evaluated periods. Missing, breaching, notBreaching and ignore have different outcomes. Composite alarms combine alarm states; they do not support Auto Scaling actions directly.
  • Use metric math for an error rate; publish both failed and total requests. Dashboards visualise data, alarms evaluate it. Cross-account observability links source accounts to a monitoring account within a Region; cross-Region dashboards are a separate capability.

Choose / compare. Choose an alarm for a recurring condition; use Logs Insights to investigate individual events. Neither creates a missing memory metric.

Try the related local exercise: alarm

Exam clue. Need an automatic response to sustained metric behaviour → alarm, then an appropriate action.

Trap. Detailed monitoring changes frequency, not the list of guest OS metrics. Composite alarms can notify or trigger supported operations; use underlying metric alarms for scaling.

Example 
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm --alarm-name high-cpu \
  --namespace AWS/EC2 --metric-name CPUUtilization \
  --dimensions Name=InstanceId,Value=i-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --statistic Average --period 60 --evaluation-periods 3 \
  --datapoints-to-alarm 2 --threshold 80 \
  --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold --treat-missing-data missing
Investigate, remediate & verify

Evidence. Check namespace, dimensions, statistic, units, period, timestamps, ingestion delay and TreatMissingData before changing the threshold. Confirm the SNS subscription and alarm actions are enabled.

Action → verification. Correct the metric or action configuration; publish a controlled test value and verify state history plus delivery. Avoid testing destructive actions against production.

Analogy. The dashboard is the instrument panel; the alarm is the rule that decides when to ring.

Canary test, custom schedule, or trace correlation? 
Scheduled canary → managed Lambda-based test → endpoint → metrics + artifacts → alarm
Existing request telemetry → correlated trace/map → investigation

CloudWatch Synthetics canaries run scheduled endpoint/browser scripts. Lambda functions perform the work underneath; Synthetics supplies monitoring integrations, metrics and test artifacts.

Scheduled Lambda can implement a custom check, but you assemble its schedule, measurements, reporting, artifact retention and alarms. Prefer the purpose-built monitor when those managed capabilities are the deciding requirement.

ServiceLens is older exam terminology for correlating metrics, logs and traces; it does not execute browser tests. Current docs combine ServiceLens/service maps into the X-Ray trace map and describe Application Signals for application observability.

CapabilityExecutes endpoint tests?What it owns
SyntheticsYes, configured canaryScheduled test + monitoring/artifacts
Scheduled LambdaYes, custom codeCustom execution; you assemble monitoring
Trace map / older ServiceLensNoCorrelates observed request telemetry
Dashboard / alarmNoDisplay / evaluate existing signals

Exam trigger. Scheduled customer-journey validation, even with no real traffic → Synthetics; investigate an existing slow request → traces/logs/correlation.

Common trap. Dashboards display evidence; metric alarms evaluate metrics; composite alarms combine alarm states. None is the endpoint test executor.

Official references: Canaries · Trace map / ServiceLens terminology

AWS references: Alarm evaluation · Missing data · Cross-account observability

Logs, queries & traces

Find the event or downstream operation behind an aggregate symptom.

Flow. Application / guest → configured collector → logs / traces → correlated query → hypothesis.

  • CloudWatch Agent collects guest logs and metrics; its IAM role, configuration, network access and log retention must be managed. Container Insights supports ECS/EKS operational telemetry.
  • A metric filter turns matching incoming log events into metric values for future alarms. Logs Insights queries retained log data; it does not retroactively populate a metric filter.
  • X-Ray/OpenTelemetry traces correlate request segments and downstream subsegments. Sampling limits volume; an absent trace is not proof that no request occurred.
  • Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus stores and queries Prometheus metrics; Amazon Managed Grafana presents dashboards. Monitor Lambda errors, duration, throttles and concurrency, plus Bedrock latency, invocation errors and quotas for AI workloads.

Choose / compare. Use logs for event detail, traces for where one request spent time and metrics for trends. Set retention and query windows to control cost.

Exam clue. Alarm says latency rose; need the slow dependency → correlated trace and application logs.

Trap. A trace is not an API audit log. Detailed EC2 monitoring does not install a log collector.

Example 
# CloudWatch Logs Insights query (query editor)
fields @timestamp, @message, requestId
| filter @message like /ERROR/
| stats count(*) as errors by bin(5m)
Investigate, remediate & verify

Evidence. Correlate timestamps, request IDs, deployment version and trace ID. Confirm agent status, log stream timestamps, IAM permissions and ingestion before interpreting an empty query.

Action → verification. Repair collection or instrumentation; reproduce one known request and confirm its log and downstream trace. Redact secrets and personal data at source.

Analogy. Metrics count late deliveries; logs record each delivery; a trace follows one parcel through the depots.

AWS references: Logs Insights · Agent · Managed Prometheus

CloudTrail & change evidence

Record supported AWS API activity: who acted, what changed and from where.

Flow. Supported AWS API activity → event record → identity/change investigation.

  • Event history provides recent management events in each Region. Trails deliver ongoing events; configure multi-Region and organisation coverage deliberately.
  • Data events, such as supported S3 object operations, require appropriate event selectors and have separate cost. A management trail is not automatically an object access log.
  • Log file validation supports integrity checking. Protect log buckets with least privilege, encryption, retention and deletion controls. Query long-term logs with Athena or supported CloudTrail analysis tools.

Choose / compare. Choose CloudTrail for API identity and change time; Config explains resource configuration history; ALB logs explain HTTP requests.

Exam clue. Who removed the ingress rule? → CloudTrail management event.

Trap. CloudTrail does not replace application logs, packet capture or a Config compliance rule.

Example 
aws cloudtrail lookup-events \
  --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=EventName,AttributeValue=AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress \
  --max-results 10
Investigate, remediate & verify

Evidence. Search around the incident for eventName, userIdentity, errorCode, requestParameters and sourceIPAddress in the correct account/Region.

Action → verification. Correct the unauthorised or accidental change through controlled tooling; verify the resource state and a new successful operation, then prevent recurrence with policy or automation.

Analogy. A signed change register, rather than a live health monitor.

AWS references: Event history · Data events

EventBridge, SNS & remediation

Turn a matching operational event into a notification or a controlled recovery action.

Flow. Operational event → matching rule → authorised target → bounded procedure → result.

  • EventBridge rules match event patterns on a bus; Scheduler handles time-based invocations. Input transformers change target input, not the source resource.
  • SNS fans notifications to subscribed endpoints; confirm subscriptions and delivery permissions. SQS buffers work with visibility timeouts, retries and dead-letter queues.
  • Use Lambda for bounded custom logic, Systems Manager Automation for a runbook and Step Functions for state, waits, retries and approvals. Standard and Express workflow semantics differ.
  • Check EventBridge target retry policy and DLQ. A DLQ is an investigation queue, not automatic successful recovery. Make actions idempotent and constrain their role.

Choose / compare. An event routes work; a runbook owns the operational procedure. Use a schedule when the requirement is a recurring time, not a resource-state transition.

Exam clue. React to a resource event → EventBridge; notify people → SNS; execute a repeatable multi-step repair → Automation.

Trap. A matched rule does not prove the target ran or that the repair worked. Avoid recursive remediation loops.

Example 
# EventBridge event-pattern excerpt
{"source":["aws.ec2"],"detail-type":["EC2 Instance State-change Notification"],
 "detail":{"state":["stopped"]}}
Investigate, remediate & verify

Evidence. Check the event bus, exact JSON pattern, MatchedEvents/FailedInvocations, target role or resource policy, DLQ and downstream execution history.

Action → verification. Test the pattern, fix target access and safely replay/reprocess eligible failures; verify the resource outcome as well as target invocation.

Analogy. The switchboard dispatches a ticket; the runbook is the repair procedure.

Notify on creation, not every transition or datapoint 
EC2 RunInstances → CloudTrail API event → EventBridge rule → SNS
Direct EC2 state event → EventBridge is a separate event path

To distinguish new launches from restarting existing instances, match the RunInstances API event in the appropriate CloudTrail/EventBridge setup. EC2 pending/running events also occur on starts of existing instances.

EventBridge also receives direct service events without CloudTrail. Choose the event that identifies the required operation rather than adding an audit dependency to every event flow.

Logs → metric filter → alarm can be appropriate for aggregated conditions, but is a more complex route for individual event notifications. Alarm notifications normally follow state transitions; repeated matching events while already ALARM are not one notification each.

# EventBridge event-pattern excerpt
{"source":["aws.ec2"],"detail-type":["AWS API Call via CloudTrail"],
 "detail":{"eventSource":["ec2.amazonaws.com"],"eventName":["RunInstances"]}}

Exam trigger. Notify about each matching new launch API operation → event pattern and target, not a metric alarm that stays ALARM.

Common trap. One RunInstances call can launch multiple instances; one matching API event is not necessarily one notification per created instance. Transform/process IDs if the requirement is per instance.

Official references: EC2 API audit · CloudTrail events in EventBridge · Alarms

AWS references: Rules · Target retries · SNS

EC2 performance & capacity

Operate instances with sufficient CPU, memory, storage and network capacity.

Flow. Healthy launch configuration → instance → workload → resource measurements → controlled replacement/tuning.

  • Distinguish instance status checks from system status checks; inspect OS logs and CloudWatch Agent metrics for guest failures.
  • T-family CPU credits can constrain sustained burst workloads. Network and EBS limits belong to the instance as well as the volume; changing only one can leave the bottleneck.
  • Use Compute Optimizer recommendations with representative workload metrics, tags and cost data. On-Demand, Spot and commitment discounts have different interruption and flexibility trade-offs.
  • Placement groups address specific latency, partition or failure-isolation needs. Capacity Reservations reserve capacity; a Savings Plan discounts eligible usage without reserving capacity.

Choose / compare. Scale horizontally when the application supports more workers; resize when a single process needs more memory/CPU. Verify licensing, restart and architecture constraints.

Exam clue. Sustained CPU plus falling credit balance on burstable instances → investigate credits and instance family.

Trap. Minimum ASG capacity is not a capacity reservation. A lower hourly price can cost more if it cannot meet the workload.

Example 
aws ec2 describe-instance-status --include-all-instances \
  --instance-ids i-0123456789abcdef0
Investigate, remediate & verify

Evidence. Compare CPU, credit balance, memory, swap, NetworkIn/Out, EBS queue/latency and service latency over the same interval. A busy CPU is a signal, not a root cause.

Action → verification. Right-size, tune or replace through the launch template and instance refresh; measure throughput and latency after warm-up and maintain a rollback version.

Analogy. Check whether the machine is short of engine power, working space or road capacity before buying a larger engine.

Resize: stop → change → start 
Compatible EBS-backed instance → stop → change instance type → start → verify

In-place resizing requires compatibility and downtime. Stopping an ASG member can cause replacement unless maintenance is coordinated with ASG behaviour.

Instance ID, private IPv4, EIP and assigned IPv6 persist across ordinary stop/start; an auto-assigned public IPv4 normally changes. Instance-store contents are lost. EBS data persists according to its lifecycle.

Resizing changes the compatible EBS-root instance’s CPU/RAM configuration, not its AMI metadata or disk size. No manual root-volume move is required. An instance-store-root workload needs migration instead of this in-place path.

An EBS-root instance can also have instance-store disks. Their data survives a normal reboot, but is lost on stop/start, termination or underlying disk failure. Copy required data to persistent storage before maintenance.

Exam trigger. Need a larger compatible instance → account for stop/start downtime and the address clients use.

Common trap. An Elastic IP and an auto-assigned public IPv4 do not have the same stop/start behaviour.

Official references: Change instance type · Stop/start effects · Instance-store lifetime

Enhanced networking: capability versus implementation 
Measure PPS / bandwidth / allowance counters → inspect instance + driver → select compatible networking

Enhanced networking uses SR-IOV; ENA is the modern implementation for Nitro-based instances. Some older families use Intel 82599 VF. Actual bandwidth/PPS constraints depend on instance type, size and traffic pattern.

An older practice explanation’s roughly 20K-PPS legacy-VIF clue is not a universal modern EC2 ceiling. Do not memorise old 10/25-Gbps figures as the limit of every current instance.

EFA targets tightly coupled HPC/AI communication. Direct Connect connects an on-premises network to AWS; neither is the general remedy for a legacy application instance’s network interface bottleneck.

Exam trigger. Legacy interface bottleneck on a compatible workload → examine enhanced networking/ENA and the exact instance limits.

Common trap. Buying bandwidth does not necessarily fix a packet-rate or single-flow limit.

Official references: Enhanced networking · Actual instance bandwidth

API termination, OS shutdown and ASG are separate 
Direct TerminateInstances → DisableApiTermination check
OS shutdown → stop OR terminate setting
ASG scale-in / unhealthy replacement → separate ASG controls

DisableApiTermination=true blocks direct EC2 console/CLI/API termination. It does not block OS-initiated termination when InstanceInitiatedShutdownBehavior=terminate, or ASG scale-in/unhealthy replacement.

With shutdown behaviour stop, OS shutdown stops the EBS-root instance; a normally operating ASG may later replace that unhealthy member. Scale-in protection is another setting and does not block unhealthy replacement.

ControlBlocksDoes not guarantee
EC2 termination protectionDirect EC2 terminationNo OS/ASG termination
Shutdown behaviour: stopSelects OS-shutdown outcomeASG keeps a stopped member
ASG scale-in protectionSelected scale-in terminationNo unhealthy replacement

Exam trigger. First identify the actor and action: direct terminate, OS shutdown, scale-in or health replacement.

Common trap. A question claiming immediate termination after shutdown assumes the terminate setting. Do not infer it from API termination protection alone.

Official references: EC2 termination protection · ASG protection

Capacity assurance versus commitment discounts 
Need launch capacity in AZ A → matching reservation
Need lower eligible usage price → RI / Savings Plan
Both requirements → compatible capacity and discount controls

A Capacity Reservation reserves matching AZ capacity, not a discount by itself. Immediate-start reservations have no fixed term; future-dated variants have commitment/cancellation conditions. Unused reserved capacity costs money; occupied capacity is not charged twice.

Eligible Regional RI/Savings Plan discounts can apply to matching Capacity Reservations. Sharing a reservation does not transfer ownership. Cluster placement groups are supported; older “no placement groups” explanations are outdated.

Savings Plans are spending commitments, not budget caps: unused commitment remains payable, while uncovered excess usage is On-Demand. Eligible Regional RIs offer size flexibility under documented platform/tenancy conditions.

OptionDiscount?Reserves capacity?Commitment / flexibility
On-Demand Capacity ReservationNot aloneSpecific AZImmediate-start: no fixed term; future-dated variants differ
Regional RIYesNo1/3 years; matching Region/configuration, eligible size flexibility
Zonal RIYesSpecific AZ1/3 years; matching AZ/configuration
EC2 Instance Savings PlanYesNo$/hour, 1/3 years; family + Region, size/OS/tenancy flexibility
Compute Savings PlanYesNo$/hour, 1/3 years; eligible EC2/Lambda/Fargate, broader family/Region flexibility

Exam trigger. Guaranteed matching AZ capacity → capacity reservation / Zonal RI; cost-only commitment → discount mechanism.

Common trap. ASG desired capacity, a Regional RI and a Savings Plan do not independently reserve AZ capacity.

Official references: Capacity Reservations · RI scope · Savings Plan flexibility · Placement groups

AWS references: Status checks · Compute Optimizer

EBS performance & snapshots

Provide persistent block storage within an Availability Zone; tune IOPS and throughput to the workload.

Flow. EC2 block I/O ↔ same-AZ volume; snapshot → separately restored volume.

  • gp2 performance is tied to size and credits; gp3 separates provisioned performance from capacity. io2 is for demanding I/O requirements. HDD types suit supported sequential workloads, not boot volumes.
  • An EBS volume attaches to compatible instances in its own AZ. Multi-Attach is a specialised supported io1/io2 option, not a general cross-AZ shared filesystem.
  • Snapshots are incremental backups managed regionally and can create volumes in another AZ. Copy snapshots to another Region when recovery requires it; check KMS access.
  • New volumes restored from snapshots may need initialisation; Fast Snapshot Restore or supported provisioned volume initialisation options change readiness/cost.

Choose / compare. Block disk → EBS. Shared files → EFS/FSx. Objects → S3. Check instance bandwidth before buying more volume IOPS.

ChoicePerformance mechanismOperational boundary
gp2IOPS tied to size; eligible burst creditsWatch credits and actual queue/latency.
gp3Provision IOPS/throughput separately from capacityInstance EBS limits still apply.
io2Provisioned IOPS for demanding workloadsCheck supported instance/volume capabilities and cost.

Exam clue. gp2 credits exhausted but disk size is already sufficient → consider gp3 performance settings.

Trap. Increasing a volume size does not automatically expand every filesystem. A completed snapshot is not a tested application restore.

Example 
# Example only: check instance/volume requirements before applying
aws ec2 modify-volume --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --volume-type gp3 --iops 6000 --throughput 250
Investigate, remediate & verify

Evidence. Correlate VolumeQueueLength, read/write latency, throughput, IOPS, BurstBalance where applicable, free space and the instance EBS limits.

Action → verification. Modify the supported volume type/performance, extend the partition/filesystem separately when growing size, then validate latency and restore a sample snapshot.

Analogy. A disk has separate capacity, operations-per-second and delivery-bandwidth limits.

Fast Snapshot Restore versus provisioned IOPS 
Snapshot (Regional) → enable FSR for destination AZ → wait Ready + credits
→ create new volume in that AZ → initialized blocks at creation

A snapshot is Regional; a working volume is AZ-specific. FSR is enabled per snapshot/AZ pair before creation and needs a ready state plus sufficient volume-creation credits. A copied or later snapshot does not automatically inherit FSR.

Within supported FSR performance capabilities, the new volume is fully initialised at creation, removing first-read lazy-loading latency. Higher provisioned IOPS does not by itself load snapshot blocks.

Modern EBS also offers a provisioned volume-initialisation rate for supported restores. That controls initialisation speed; it is not a promise that the new volume is fully ready instantly. Check current support, quotas and cost.

Enable FSR for the destination AZ, regardless of the original volume’s AZ. Charges run per snapshot per enabled AZ, per minute with a one-hour minimum, even without a restore; normal snapshot/volume charges remain separate. It improves first-I/O readiness, not simply API creation speed.

Exam trigger. First-read restore latency with immediate full initialisation required → prepare suitable FSR before volume creation.

Common trap. “Preload in the AZ” is a mental model, not AWS’s documented internal storage implementation. Enabling FSR after creating the affected volume does not retroactively initialise it.

Official references: FSR · Volume initialisation

Available volume, but attachment is stuck 
Volume ID → AttachVolume device mapping → driver / OS device → mount

The volume ID, requested attachment name and guest-visible device name are different identifiers. Drivers, especially NVMe enumeration, can remap names; use volume IDs/stable filesystem identifiers to identify the intended disk.

If evidence points to a retained/busy device name after a detach, verify the guest’s devices and retry with an unused supported name. Also check same-AZ placement, attachment limits and actual attachment state before choosing a remedy.

# Guest diagnostic example, Linux
lsblk -o NAME,SERIAL,SIZE,MOUNTPOINTS
# Compare with AWS volume ID/attachment mapping; do not format an unknown disk.

Exam trigger. Driver/device-name collision → unused supported mapping, not more disk performance credits.

Common trap. IOPS credits affect I/O performance, not whether the control plane can attach a disk. A stuck attachment alone does not prove which cause applies.

Official references: Attach volumes · Device naming · NVMe identifiers

Snapshot automation: lifecycle, central backup or five-minute API calls? 
rate(5 minutes) → EventBridge Scheduler execution role → EC2 CreateSnapshot
→ asynchronous snapshot completion → separate retention / deletion controls

DLM manages EBS snapshot creation/retention/deletion through the EC2 console or APIs. DLM custom schedules and AWS Backup scheduled snapshot rules have a one-hour minimum; supported continuous backup is a separate mechanism.

For every few minutes, use EventBridge Scheduler with a supported EC2 universal API target and execution role. Lambda is optional custom logic, not a mandatory hop or the schedule itself.

“CloudWatch Events” is historical terminology. Modern flexible schedules use EventBridge Scheduler. Scheduling creates recovery points but does not by itself implement retention, exact completion times or application-consistent capture. DLM cannot automatically adopt snapshots created by unrelated mechanisms.

RequirementBest fit
EBS snapshot creation, retention, deletion; hourly or less frequentData Lifecycle Manager
Central backup management across services/accounts/RegionsAWS Backup
Snapshot creation every few minutes / flexible API schedulingEventBridge Scheduler
# Scheduler target excerpt (JSON), not a complete deployment
{"Arn":"arn:aws:scheduler:::aws-sdk:ec2:createSnapshot",
 "RoleArn":"arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/snapshot-scheduler",
 "Input":"{\"VolumeId\":\"vol-0123456789abcdef0\"}"}
# ScheduleExpression: rate(5 minutes); FlexibleTimeWindow: {"Mode":"OFF"}

Exam trigger. Explicit every-five-minutes snapshot API requirement → Scheduler; built-in hourly lifecycle → DLM.

Common trap. Do not claim the EC2 console lacks automated snapshots, or that Lambda alone supplies recurrence.

Official references: DLM frequency · DLM ownership · AWS Backup frequency · Universal API targets · Legacy terminology

AWS references: Volume types · Snapshots

S3 operations & protection

Operate object storage with appropriate access, lifecycle, transfer and recovery controls.

Flow. Authorised object request → bucket/object version → response; lifecycle and recovery are separate operations.

  • Use multipart upload for suitable large objects; abort incomplete uploads with lifecycle rules. Transfer Acceleration can help long-distance uploads; benchmark before enabling it. DataSync automates supported bulk transfers.
  • Lifecycle transitions and expiration manage storage cost, subject to minimum durations, request/retrieval charges and retrieval latency. Versioning preserves older versions; a delete marker is not destruction of every version.
  • SRR/CRR replicate eligible new objects after configuration; use Batch Replication for existing objects. Replication needs versioning, permissions and encryption configuration. Lifecycle actions are not simply copied to the destination.
  • Keep access-log destination separate to avoid recursive logging. Block Public Access, bucket policies and Object Ownership govern access; an endpoint policy alone does not grant bucket access.

Choose / compare. Versioning recovers an overwritten object; replication maintains another copy; AWS Backup and Object Lock address different retention/recovery needs.

Exam clue. Recover overwritten data → version ID; copy existing objects under a replication policy → Batch Replication.

Trap. Replication can copy unwanted changes and is not an independent historical backup. Storage class changes can alter recovery time and cost.

Example 
aws s3api list-object-versions --bucket example-orders --prefix invoices/
# Retrieve an explicitly selected version (replace placeholders)
aws s3api get-object --bucket example-orders --key invoices/42.pdf \
  --version-id VERSION_ID recovered.pdf
Investigate, remediate & verify

Evidence. For 403: inspect principal, bucket/access-point policy, explicit denies, KMS access and endpoint restrictions. For slow transfers: check request concurrency, object sizes and network path.

Action → verification. Restore the required version or correct access/transfer settings; verify checksum, version ID, encryption and an application read. Test recovery from accidental deletion.

Analogy. Version history is a filing cabinet; replication is a second cabinet that follows configured changes.

Retain until is not delete at 
Versioning + Object Lock → retain protected version → retention expires
→ version becomes eligible → configured Lifecycle action eventually deletes eligible data

Object Lock protects object versions. Retain Until Date ending makes a version deletable under the applicable policies; it does not itself schedule deletion. Legal holds and remaining controls can still block it.

Use versioning and an appropriate retention mode for the stated requirement, then Lifecycle for eligible expiration/cleanup. Include noncurrent versions and delete markers in the design. Governance bypass and compliance retention have different rules.

“Keep for five years” describes a requirement; it does not prove the existing bucket already has Object Lock configured.

Exam trigger. Cannot delete before retention + automatic cleanup afterwards → retention control plus suitable lifecycle/version rules.

Common trap. Lifecycle does not bypass an active lock, and a simple delete marker does not erase a retained version.

Official references: Object Lock · Lifecycle and Object Lock

API audit and server access logging are different evidence 
Management API → CloudTrail management event
GetObject / PutObject → explicitly selected CloudTrail data events
Bucket access request → best-effort server access log delivery

S3 object-level CloudTrail data events must be explicitly configured and are charged separately; a management trail does not automatically include them.

For server access logging delivered directly to an S3 bucket there is no additional log-delivery charge; storage, access and analysis still cost money. Delivery is best effort and should not be treated as a complete immediate audit feed. Keep the source and log destination separate.

Current AWS documentation also offers CloudWatch Logs delivery with vended-log ingestion pricing. Do not generalise the S3 delivery pricing statement to every log destination.

Exam trigger. Need object API caller evidence → configure data-event coverage; compare the required completeness and costs.

Common trap. “No delivery fee” does not mean free storage or guaranteed complete real-time delivery.

Official references: CloudTrail data events · Server access logging

Physical import ends in S3, then Lifecycle 
Ship device → copy on premises → return device → AWS imports to S3
→ configured Lifecycle transition → eligible S3 Glacier storage class

Snowball Edge import moves locally copied data back to AWS before the S3 import completes. A Lifecycle rule then controls eligible storage-class transitions; the device does not directly deliver objects into a Glacier-class archive.

Availability caveat: since 7 November 2025, Snowball Edge is available only to existing customers. Treat older exam scenarios accordingly; new customers should evaluate current online/physical-transfer alternatives.

Exam trigger. An eligible existing customer needs offline bulk import, then archive storage → device import to S3 plus Lifecycle.

Common trap. Shipping, import completion and a later storage-class transition are different stages.

Official references: Availability / import process

AWS references: Versioning · Lifecycle · Replication

EFS, FSx & S3 Files

Choose and operate shared storage by protocol, application semantics and recovery needs.

Flow. Application file call → configured mount/identity → shared filesystem → result.

  • Regional EFS provides shared NFS access through mount targets in selected AZs; permit NFS and resolve the mount DNS name. EFS One Zone has a different resilience boundary.
  • FSx offerings serve specific filesystem workloads, such as Windows SMB, Lustre, ONTAP and OpenZFS. Match protocol, deployment model, throughput and snapshots/backup support. For supported Windows workloads, file version recovery can involve configured shadow copies; distinguish file-level versions from whole-filesystem backups.
  • S3 Files provides file access to S3 data through a managed filesystem; inspect its access, consistency and storage-class behaviour rather than treating an object bucket as an ordinary block disk.
  • Use lifecycle and throughput settings deliberately. Storage Gateway supports hybrid access patterns; DataSync moves supported data, rather than replacing the live application filesystem.

Choose / compare. Shared Linux files across AZs → regional EFS; Windows-specific SMB/AD requirements → suitable FSx. Choose object APIs when file semantics are unnecessary.

NeedCandidateCheck before choosing
Shared Linux NFSRegional EFSMount targets, NFS access, throughput and lifecycle.
Specific SMB / Lustre / ONTAP / OpenZFS semanticsAppropriate FSx offeringProtocol, identity, deployment/backup model.
File access over S3 dataS3 FilesSupported access/consistency and object storage-class behaviour.
Per-instance block diskEBSSame-AZ attachment; not general cross-AZ file sharing.

Exam clue. Multiple instances need the same persistent files across AZs → a regional shared filesystem.

Trap. EBS is not a general cross-AZ shared filesystem. An S3 Glacier object may require restoration before S3 Files can read it.

Example 
# NFS example with amazon-efs-utils installed; mount target/network access required
sudo mount -t efs -o tls fs-0123456789abcdef0:/ /mnt/shared
Investigate, remediate & verify

Evidence. Check mount target placement, DNS, NFS/SMB security rules, client identity, throughput mode, storage latency and application access pattern.

Action → verification. Correct mounts/access or throughput, test concurrent access from both AZs and perform a supported backup/restore test.

Analogy. EBS is a machine’s disk; a shared filesystem is a network filing room; S3 is an object repository.

AWS references: EFS mounting · FSx · S3 Files

Auto Scaling & elasticity

Reconcile a group’s running capacity with desired capacity across configured AZs.

Flow. Metric / schedule → scaling policy → desired capacity → instance reconciliation → target health.

  • Min/max constrain desired capacity. Scaling policies change desired capacity; the ASG launches or terminates instances to reconcile actual capacity. Launches still depend on subnet IPs, quotas and available capacity.
  • Target tracking follows a proportional utilisation metric; step scaling uses alarm severity. Scheduled actions handle known times; predictive scaling uses supported forecast patterns.
  • Enable ELB health checks when the group must replace application-unhealthy targets. Use health-check grace periods and instance warm-up appropriately; they solve different timing problems.
  • Lifecycle hooks allow controlled launch/termination work. Instance refresh rolls out launch-template changes; configure healthy percentages, checkpoints and rollback.

Choose / compare. ASG manages instance count/health replacement; ALB distributes requests. A single ASG is regional and can span AZs, not Regions.

Try the related local exercise: capacity

Exam clue. Predictable morning surge → scheduled scaling; changing utilisation → target tracking with a suitable metric.

Trap. Min=1 permits a single instance and does not ensure AZ redundancy. Low average CPU can hide a hot instance or a downstream bottleneck.

Example 
# Example: actual 3, desired 5; ChangeInCapacity +3 → desired 8 (if max permits)
aws autoscaling describe-scaling-activities --auto-scaling-group-name orders-asg
Investigate, remediate & verify

Evidence. Inspect scaling activities, suspended processes, desired versus InService capacity, launch-template version, subnet free IPs, health type and warm-up.

Action → verification. Repair the failing launch/health dependency, then verify capacity reaches desired and the new targets pass application checks under load.

Analogy. The ASG is the staffing manager; the load balancer allocates incoming work.

Scale-in protection: target count can differ from actual 
Policy lowers desired 4 → 3 → every member protected → actual remains 4
Remove selected protection → ASG can converge to desired

Desired capacity is a target. Scale-in protection can prevent the selected termination without preventing the target from decreasing. Inspect Activity history and actual member states.

Scale-in protection does not prevent unhealthy replacement. Group metrics must be enabled to publish the group series; use instance metrics for the individual machine.

MetricMeaning
GroupDesiredCapacityTarget capacity
GroupInServiceInstancesIn-service count
GroupPendingInstancesLaunching count
GroupTotalInstancesTotal, including in-service, pending and terminating
aws autoscaling describe-scaling-activities --auto-scaling-group-name orders

Exam trigger. Desired fell but no instance was removed → inspect scale-in protection and scaling activity.

Common trap. An in-service count is not a guarantee that every application is healthy; health/replacement is a separate process.

Official references: Protection · Group metrics

AWS references: Scaling policies · Health checks

Load balancing & target health

Accept traffic on listeners and route it to registered targets using rules and health information.

Flow. Client → listener → matching rule → target group → selected target → response.

  • ALB routes HTTP/HTTPS by host/path and other supported rules; NLB handles supported transport-layer requirements. Internet-facing frontends can reach private backend targets.
  • ALB cross-zone is on at load-balancer level; target-group settings can disable it. With cross-zone and equivalent targets, 2 in AZ A plus 8 in B means roughly 10% per target, not 50% per AZ.
  • Health checks use configured port, path, timeout, matcher and thresholds. A service can work directly yet fail its health check. If all targets are unhealthy, ALB can fail open.
  • Deregistration delay drains connections. Sticky sessions, routing algorithm and differing response times can create unequal request counts.

Choose / compare. Need HTTP routing → ALB. Need instance replacement → ASG with the relevant health checks. Need cross-Region entry/failover → DNS or Global Accelerator as appropriate.

Try the related local exercise: capacity · network

Exam clue. Requests fail only through the load balancer → compare health configuration, target rules and frontend/backend security.

Trap. Cross-zone distributes eligible traffic, not guaranteed equal request counts. An ALB is regional; it does not span Regions.

Example 
aws elbv2 describe-target-health --target-group-arn TARGET_GROUP_ARN
# Illustration: browser → HTTPS:443 listener → /orders rule → HTTP:8080 target
Investigate, remediate & verify

Evidence. Inspect target-health reason, ALB versus target 5xx, TargetResponseTime and access logs. Check listener rule, target port, SG references and health endpoint dependencies.

Action → verification. Correct the first failing boundary; verify repeated healthy checks, request success and latency. Do not make the health endpoint lie to hide a broken dependency.

Analogy. The receptionist routes visitors; the building manager replaces a broken office.

Health status is periodic; HTTP status is a request outcome 
Periodic probes → target health → eligible routing
Separate request → selected target → HTTP result

ALB does not run a fresh health check before every request. It uses periodically evaluated target health. With healthy targets available it normally avoids unhealthy ones; all registered targets unhealthy can cause fail-open routing.

Unhealthy does not automatically mean HTTP 503. No registered targets/all targets unused can produce an ALB 503; a backend application can independently return its own 503. Read target-health reasons and ALB versus target status evidence.

ASG uses enabled ELB health checks to replace the failed instance; it does not simply restart that application. One failed AZ is not necessarily every target failing: inspect healthy targets, cross-zone settings and whether there is one load balancer or several.

Exam trigger. Separate health state, routing eligibility, actual request status and ASG replacement.

Common trap. A periodic health result can lag a new failure; all-unhealthy fail-open is not a guarantee of successful responses.

Official references: ALB health · ALB HTTP errors · ASG health

AWS references: Health checks · Cross-zone

RDS, Aurora & database recovery

Operate relational availability, read scaling, connections, performance and recovery.

Flow. Application → chosen writer/read endpoint → SQL result; replication and historical recovery are separate paths.

  • A traditional Multi-AZ DB instance has a synchronous standby for failover, not read traffic. A Multi-AZ DB cluster has readable instances; Aurora has its own replicated storage and reader architecture.
  • Read replicas generally replicate asynchronously; route reads to their endpoints and monitor lag. Aurora Serverless v2 adjusts supported database capacity within configured limits; it does not remove query tuning.
  • Use CloudWatch Database Insights to analyse DB load, waits and SQL. Older study material calls out Performance Insights. RDS Proxy pools/manages connections; it does not repair inefficient SQL.
  • Automated backups support PITR within configured retention, up to 35 days for supported RDS DB instances. Manual snapshots persist until deleted. Restore creates a new database resource; plan endpoint cutover and KMS access.

Choose / compare. Host/AZ failure → Multi-AZ; read pressure with lag tolerance → read replicas; accidental logical change → PITR/snapshot restore.

CapabilityPrimarily solvesImportant limit
Traditional Multi-AZ instanceHost/AZ failoverOne standby is not a reader.
Multi-AZ DB cluster / Aurora deploymentAvailability with readable instancesInspect the specified deployment/endpoint model.
Read replicaRead scalingAsynchronous lag; application selects read endpoint.
PITR / snapshot restoreHistorical recoveryNew resource; validate and plan cutover.
RDS ProxyConnection managementDoes not fix inefficient SQL or transaction locks.

Try the related local exercise: recovery

Exam clue. Deleted valid rows but database remains healthy → PITR, not a standby that replicated the deletion.

Trap. Failover is not historical recovery. A successful restore API response does not mean the new endpoint is ready or validated.

Example 
aws rds restore-db-instance-to-point-in-time \
  --source-db-instance-identifier orders-db \
  --target-db-instance-identifier orders-recovered \
  --restore-time 2026-11-09T01:25:00Z
Investigate, remediate & verify

Evidence. Compare CPU, FreeableMemory, storage latency/free space, connections, replica lag and DB-load waits. Check events and pending modifications/maintenance windows.
