Action → verification. Tune SQL/indexes or the limiting resource; test failover with reconnect logic. Restore to an isolated DB, validate records and redirect traffic only after checks.

Analogy. A standby replaces a failed shop; a backup recovers the ledger from before a bad entry.

MySQL replica: endpoint, writes & message limits 
Application writes → source endpoint → asynchronous replication → replica
Reporting reads → replica’s own endpoint

Each RDS instance has its own endpoint. MySQL read replicas normally reject application writes with read_only enabled. Setting read_only=0 permits writes, but conflicting changes can stop replication; a replica is not a second independently writable primary.

A replica-specific index is a documented special case requiring read_only=0 while it is created. Do not generalise that exception into permission for arbitrary application writes.

max_allowed_packet bounds an individual logical MySQL message, such as a statement, row or replication event. It is neither database capacity nor total transaction/write volume. A large message can break replication when the replica’s configured value is lower; matching source/replica parameter values removes that mismatch.

# Read-only diagnostic SQL; connect to the intended instance endpoint
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'read_only';
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'max_allowed_packet';

Exam trigger. Replication stopped with a packet-size error → compare parameter groups and the failing logical message.

Common trap. A lower limit need not fail immediately: the problematic message must arrive. A MySQL logical message is not one Ethernet/TCP packet.

Official references: RDS replication troubleshooting · MySQL logical packets

AWS references: Multi-AZ · PITR · Database Insights · Backup retention

DynamoDB scaling & recovery

Operate a managed key-value database by access pattern, partition pressure and recovery policy.

Flow. Key-based request → table / index capacity → result; recovery creates a new table.

  • On-demand manages request capacity; provisioned mode uses configured RCU/WCU with optional Auto Scaling. Auto Scaling reacts to usage and is not instantaneous.
  • A hot partition key can throttle even when table totals appear low. Inspect throttling reason, key distribution and GSI capacity; a GSI with insufficient write capacity can back-pressure table writes.
  • DAX accelerates supported eventually consistent reads with a compatible client; strong reads bypass its cache to DynamoDB. Global tables replicate across Regions; they do not provide historical undo.
  • Enable PITR for supported continuous recovery and use on-demand/AWS Backup snapshots for retention requirements. Restore produces a new table; recheck dependent settings and application routing.

Choose / compare. Variable unpredictable traffic → consider on-demand; predictable demand → provisioned plus scaling. Correct hot keys before blindly increasing total capacity.

Exam clue. Throttles despite low aggregate utilisation → inspect partitions/indexes, not only table totals.

Trap. TTL deletion is asynchronous; it is not a precise scheduler. Replication does not preserve every previous valid value.

Example 
aws dynamodb describe-continuous-backups --table-name Orders
aws dynamodb describe-table --table-name Orders
Investigate, remediate & verify

Evidence. Inspect consumed/provisioned capacity, throttles by table/index, latency, failed conditions and Contributor Insights hot-key evidence where enabled.

Action → verification. Adjust capacity or access pattern, verify per-key success and tail latency; test restore and switch the application to the validated new table.

Analogy. A warehouse can have free space overall while one busy loading bay is overloaded.

AWS references: Capacity · PITR

ElastiCache & cache operations

Reduce repeated database work while managing freshness, eviction and failure behaviour.

Flow. Read → cache hit, or miss → database → cache population; write/invalidation follows the selected strategy.

  • Valkey/Redis OSS shards partition data; replicas copy their shard asynchronously and support reads/failover in suitable configurations. More replicas do not spread primary writes across shards.
  • Node-based Memcached provides a simpler distributed cache without Redis OSS-style primary/replica failover. Serverless and node-based models differ in scaling, controls and pricing; inspect the chosen deployment model.
  • Cache-aside populates on a miss; TTL expires entries without refreshing them. Write-through updates database/cache in a coordinated application workflow; invalidation removes the cached value after a database change.
  • Track hit rate, evictions, memory, engine CPU, connections and replication lag. A cache outage can suddenly push the entire read load onto the database.

Choose / compare. HTTP objects at the edge → CloudFront; DynamoDB-compatible cache → DAX; custom sessions/computed values → ElastiCache.

Exam clue. Read-heavy repeated values with acceptable staleness → caching; write pressure → examine shards and workload, not just replicas.

Trap. TTL expiration does not refresh data, and database/cache writes are not automatically atomic.

Example 
# Cache-aside pseudocode
value = cache.get("product:42")
if value is None:
    value = database.read(42)
    cache.set("product:42", value, ttl=60)
Investigate, remediate & verify

Evidence. Check whether misses, hot keys, memory pressure or a node failure preceded database load. Compare DB and cached values before assuming a stale response is a DB issue.

Action → verification. Tune TTL/invalidation, memory or shard capacity; test failover and cold-cache load. Use bounded retries and protect the source database.

Analogy. A desk copy saves trips to the archive, but someone must decide when that copy is too old.

AWS references: ElastiCache · Caching strategies · Engine comparison

AWS Backup & disaster recovery

Schedule protected recovery points, manage retention/copies and prove that recovery works.

Flow. Protected resource → recovery point → optional copy → restore → application/data validation.

  • Backup plans select resources by explicit assignment or tags; check roles, supported resource settings and job outcomes. Copy to another account/Region when the recovery requirement calls for it.
  • Vault Lock protects retention with governance/compliance semantics; compliance mode becomes immutable after its grace period. Choose deliberately before committing retention controls.
  • Restore testing exercises supported restores and validation. An available recovery point says little about application readiness, permissions, dependencies or actual RTO.
  • Backup/restore, pilot light, warm standby and active/active trade ongoing cost against recovery work. RTO is tolerable outage; RPO is tolerable lost time of data. Both require measurement.

Choose / compare. Choose the least costly tested procedure that meets both objectives; replication/failover handles availability but can replicate corruption.

Try the related local exercise: recovery

Exam clue. Keep recoverable history outside the workload account → controlled cross-account backup copies and tested access.

Trap. Replication is not a backup. No universal RTO belongs to a DR label; recovery time depends on the actual tested procedure.

Example 
aws backup list-backup-jobs --by-state FAILED
aws backup list-recovery-points-by-backup-vault --backup-vault-name orders-vault
Investigate, remediate & verify

Evidence. Inspect backup/copy/restore job status, last recoverable timestamp, vault/account/Region, encryption grants, retention and application dependency order.

Action → verification. Restore into isolation, validate business records and integrations, time the full cutover and clean up test resources. Record the demonstrated RTO/RPO.

Analogy. A spare building is useful only if the recovery team has the keys and has practised opening it.

AWS references: Backup plans · Restore testing · Vault Lock · DR strategies

CloudFormation & CDK lifecycle

Maintain declared resources through reviewed stack changes and controlled failure recovery.

Flow. Template (optionally CDK synthesis) → reviewed stack operation → resource events → health verification.

  • CDK synthesises templates and assets; CloudFormation provisions the stack. Change sets preview supported changes and replacements; they do not guarantee an update will succeed.
  • Read stack events from the first relevant failure. UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED requires repairing the rollback cause and continuing rollback. Skipping resources is a last resort and leaves reconciliation work.
  • Drift detection compares supported resource properties to the template; it does not automatically repair drift or inspect every property. DeletionPolicy and UpdateReplacePolicy protect different deletion/replacement moments.
  • StackSets distribute stacks across accounts/Regions with permissions, concurrency and failure-tolerance controls. Parameters are inputs; conditions choose resources/properties; DependsOn orders dependencies.

Choose / compare. Need repeatable infrastructure → a stack; preview a change → change set; distribute the template → StackSets; share an existing supported resource → RAM.

Try the related local exercise: stack

Exam clue. Stack stuck in UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED → fix cause, then continue-update-rollback.

Trap. Deleting a failed production stack is not a routine recovery step. A change set is a preview, not an executed deployment.

Example 
aws cloudformation describe-stack-events --stack-name orders
# After fixing the specific rollback cause:
aws cloudformation continue-update-rollback --stack-name orders
Investigate, remediate & verify

Evidence. Inspect resource status reason, service role, quotas, subnet IP capacity, name collisions, missing exports and replacement dependencies. Distinguish update failure from rollback failure.

Action → verification. Fix the prerequisite, continue rollback where appropriate, review the next change set and verify stack status plus application health. Reconcile any skipped resource before another update.

Analogy. The template is the agreed building plan; drift is a room changed outside that plan.

IAM, stack policy, termination protection or Retain? 
Caller IAM → UpdateStack → separate stack-policy check → resource changes / failure

A stack policy is a separate JSON document attached to the stack. It restricts updates to existing logical resources even when IAM permits UpdateStack. Update:Modify, Update:Replace and Update:Delete describe update actions; Update:* covers all three.

A prohibited change fails the update; CloudFormation does not silently skip it and report success. An authorised operator can supply a temporary override for an intentional protected update. Other resources may already have changed before a later permission failure; rollback can fail or be disabled.

RequirementControl
Restrict existing-resource updatesStack policy
Block deletion of the entire stackStack termination protection
Keep a resource when deleting its stackDeletionPolicy: Retain
Authorise/restrict direct AWS API actionsIAM policies
# Separate stack-policy excerpt, not template YAML
{"Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow","Action":"Update:*","Principal":"*","Resource":"*"},
 {"Effect":"Deny","Action":"Update:Replace","Principal":"*","Resource":"LogicalResourceId/Database"}]}

Exam trigger. Protect a database during stack updates → stack policy; first identify which operation must be blocked.

Common trap. A stack policy is neither an IAM permission grant nor protection against direct service API calls.

Official references: Stack policies

Regional stacks, account-wide names 
Sydney stack creates a named IAM role → another Region tries the same name → conflict
Alternative: generate a unique name OR explicitly reference the one owned resource

IAM role/user names are account-wide, not shared across every AWS account. CloudFormation stacks are Regional: a second stack does not silently adopt an existing role with the same RoleName.

Omit optional physical names, or include Region/stack identifiers. Intentional sharing needs one owner and an ARN input/reference; importing a resource is a separate explicit workflow.

S3 buckets are Regional too, but traditional general-purpose bucket names share a namespace across accounts/Regions within a partition. Current S3 also supports optional account-Regional namespaces with a prescribed name suffix.

# Template excerpt for a NEW role, not a reference to an existing role
RoleName: !Sub "${AWS::StackName}-${AWS::Region}-app"
# For intentional reuse, take an ExistingRoleArn parameter instead.

Exam trigger. Same template fails only in the second Region with AlreadyExists → check account-wide physical names.

Common trap. Referencing an ARN does not create a second resource. A late create failure does not prove earlier resources were never created.

Official references: Named IAM roles · S3 namespaces

AWS references: Rollback recovery · Drift · StackSets

Images & deployment operations

Promote tested machine/container artifacts and update an existing deployment safely.

Flow. Build → test → registry / AMI distribution → controlled rollout → health gate.

  • EC2 Image Builder automates build, test and distribution of AMIs/container images. An AMI is regional; copying encrypted images requires compatible KMS permissions.
  • ECR stores images; ECS/EKS run containers. Check image URI/digest, pull permissions, platform architecture, registry connectivity, task/pod events, probes and resource limits.
  • Use immutable digests for repeatable releases. Rolling changes existing capacity in batches; blue/green retains another environment during cutover. Account for database compatibility and rollback.
  • Git records changes; Terraform plans/applies its managed resources with protected remote state and locking. Avoid two IaC tools independently owning the same resource.

Choose / compare. Image creation/distribution → Image Builder/ECR; workload rollout → the existing ASG/ECS/EKS/deployment service. Operate the chosen pipeline rather than redesigning one for this exam.

Exam clue. Same fault on every replacement instance → investigate the image/template/config, not repeated manual instance repair.

Trap. An uploaded image is not a running task. A mutable latest tag makes rollback provenance harder to prove.

Example 
aws ecs describe-services --cluster orders --services orders-api
aws ecr describe-images --repository-name orders-api
Investigate, remediate & verify

Evidence. For failed deployment, start at events and the first unhealthy dependency: subnet IP exhaustion, image pull, permissions, startup command, health probe or application config.

Action → verification. Correct the dependency and redeploy a pinned artifact with a controlled rollout; verify new revision, healthy count, error rate and rollback readiness.

Analogy. The image is a sealed installation kit; deployment decides where and when that kit runs.

AMI ≠ working disk ≠ Launch Template 
Working EBS → snapshot
AMI = boot metadata + snapshot references
Launch Template = AMI ID + instance/network/storage settings
Launch → fresh EBS volumes from snapshots → new instance

Boot metadata includes architecture, root-device mappings, virtualisation type and boot mode. An EBS-backed AMI refers to snapshots; it is not the live volume still attached to the source instance.

ASG launches normally create new root volumes from the image’s snapshots. Reattaching an existing data disk is a different explicit workflow. A replacement AMI can be created from a running/stopped instance or a suitable retained root snapshot with matching boot settings.

Exam trigger. Need repeatable replacement instances → usable image plus launch configuration, not a plan to move one root disk between every launch.

Common trap. A snapshot is disk data; it does not alone specify every boot setting or the desired EC2 instance type.

Official references: EBS-backed AMIs · Launch Templates

Image consistency and deregistration recovery 
Coordinate application writes → flush/freeze or allow reboot → capture image → test boot AND data
Deregistered AMI → matching pre-existing Recycle Bin rule? → restore within retention

Durable captured blocks do not automatically prove application consistency. Allowing the image-creation reboot helps flush buffered state; transactional applications can need their own quiesce/backup coordination. “Disable No reboot” means allow reboot.

An accidentally deregistered eligible EBS-backed AMI can be recovered through Recycle Bin when a matching retention rule already applied and retention has not expired. Otherwise investigate retained snapshots or a surviving instance; reconstruct with correct boot settings.

Exam trigger. Before-image consistency requirements and recoverable historical artifacts change the recovery answer.

Common trap. “Deregistered means never recoverable” is outdated. A retention rule created after the deletion does not retroactively save an unretained image.

Official references: Image capture · Deregister / Recycle Bin

AZ, account and Region are separate sharing boundaries 
Another AZ: same Regional AMI
Another account: AMI launch permission + eligible encryption access
Another Region: copy image, then share/use the destination copy

Sharing the AMI permits use of its backing snapshots for launching without separately sharing those snapshots. Copying a shared AMI can require additional read permissions for its backing storage.

Encrypted sharing needs a customer-managed KMS key with suitable cross-account permissions. An image encrypted under the default AWS-managed aws/ebs key cannot simply be shared cross-account. Copy/re-encrypt under an appropriate customer-managed key when required.

Another account and Region involves both sharing/access permissions and a destination-Region copy. Same-account cross-Region copying is not prohibited merely because the source used the AWS-managed aws/ebs key; use an appropriate destination-Region encryption key.

A KMS multi-Region key has distinct Regional primary/replica resources. Ordinary customer-managed keys are not global, and Region copying is a separate boundary from cross-account key sharing.

Exam trigger. Launching a shared image and copying it have different backing-snapshot permission requirements.

Common trap. Cross-account use does not imply cross-Region copying; name the changed boundary first.

Official references: Sharing images · Copying images · Cross-Region image copies

Baked agent: installed is not sending 
AMI with agent/config → fresh instance → automatic startup + IAM + endpoints → telemetry

The image supplies the installed CloudWatch Agent and configuration to each launch. ASG does not independently install software merely because it launches the AMI.

Publishing still needs startup, a valid instance role, correct configuration/dimensions and endpoint access. Validate a new instance’s own log/metric stream, not only the old source instance’s telemetry.

# Linux diagnostic example
systemctl status amazon-cloudwatch-agent
# Check agent logs, instance-role permissions and HTTPS endpoint reachability.

Exam trigger. Agent baked into image but new instance has no guest metrics → check startup, permissions and connectivity.

Common trap. EC2 basic metrics can exist while memory/disk-space or application logs are missing.

Official references: CloudWatch Agent

AWS references: Image Builder · ECS troubleshooting · ECR

Systems Manager operations

Inventory, connect to, patch, configure and automate managed resources.

Flow. Authorised operator / event → runbook → scoped API or managed-node operation → recorded outcome.

  • Managed nodes need an agent where applicable, instance/service permissions and network connectivity. Session Manager avoids opening inbound SSH/RDP; configure session logging and access explicitly.
  • Run Command performs supported commands; Automation runbooks coordinate operational steps/API calls with optional approvals. State Manager maintains desired associations; Patch Manager handles patch baselines/operations.
  • Maintenance Windows schedule controlled maintenance. Parameter Store holds configuration and SecureString values; Secrets Manager adds supported secret rotation workflows.
  • Limit automation concurrency and error thresholds. Multi-account/Region execution needs trusted roles and target access; an automation service role is separate from a node’s role.

Choose / compare. One command on managed nodes → Run Command; a repair procedure with branching/approval → Automation; ongoing desired setup → State Manager.

Exam clue. Repeat a repair with approvals and auditability → Automation runbook.

Trap. The console showing a node does not prove it is currently online. A successful command exit code is not an application health test.

Example 
aws ssm describe-instance-information
# Example runbook; review its steps and target before execution
aws ssm start-automation-execution --document-name AWS-RestartEC2Instance \
  --parameters InstanceId=i-0123456789abcdef0
Investigate, remediate & verify

Evidence. For an offline node, inspect agent service/version, instance role, DNS/proxy, time, and outbound HTTPS to required endpoints. No inbound SSH rule is required for Session Manager.

Action → verification. Restore management connectivity, target a safe tag group, dry-run/test where supported, then verify command/runbook output and actual service health.

Analogy. A managed workshop: access, tool inventory, maintenance schedule and repeatable repair instructions.

Agent management versus offline EC2Rescue 
Online: agent + node IAM + outbound HTTPS → SSM
Offline rescue: Automation → temporary helper → detached root EBS → repair → reattach

Ordinary agent-based management requires a working agent, credentials/permissions and outbound endpoint connectivity. Automation is broader: its runbooks can call AWS APIs without executing inside the impaired OS.

AWSSupport-ExecuteEC2Rescue can orchestrate an offline workflow using temporary helper resources and the impaired instance’s root EBS volume. Review the runbook’s prerequisites, permissions, backup and stop/restart behaviour. This is not an agent command somehow running inside an unreachable OS.

Use repair when preserving/fixing this instance matters. An ASG generally replaces an unhealthy instance; guard against that replacement interfering with intentional repair or maintenance.

Exam trigger. Agent unreachable and root-volume repair required → appropriate offline rescue runbook, not repeated Run Command.

Common trap. An installed agent is not evidence it is currently running or connected.

Official references: EC2Rescue runbook · Automation

AWS references: Automation · Session Manager · Patch Manager

Multi-account operations

Apply approved governance and share or deploy resources across account and Region boundaries.

Flow. Baseline → StackSet instances; existing supported resource → RAM share; access → IAM plus guardrails.

  • Organizations organises accounts/OUs; SCPs restrict applicable member-account permissions and never grant access. IAM Identity Center provides workforce federation and permission-set access.
  • Control Tower establishes/governs a landing zone; Service Catalog distributes approved products. RAM shares supported existing resources, such as subnets, without cloning every resource.
  • StackSets deploys template instances; regional settings and service availability still matter. Track execution roles, delegated administration, organisational units and excluded accounts.
  • Use tags, Cost Explorer and Cost and Usage Reports to identify waste and ownership; check Compute Optimizer/Trusted Advisor recommendations against workload requirements. Savings Plans are discounts, not capacity guarantees.

Choose / compare. Replicate infrastructure → StackSets; share a resource → RAM; limit allowed operations → SCP; grant a workforce session → Identity Center plus permission policies.

Exam clue. Same baseline in many accounts/Regions → StackSets; share existing subnets → RAM.

Trap. An SCP allow does not grant an IAM permission. Cost optimisation must preserve availability and recovery constraints.

Example 
aws cloudformation list-stack-instances --stack-set-name baseline
aws organizations list-policies-for-target --target-id ACCOUNT_ID \
  --filter SERVICE_CONTROL_POLICY
Investigate, remediate & verify

Evidence. When one account fails, compare OU/SCP inheritance, role trust, service-linked roles, Region enablement, quotas and target resource policies.

Action → verification. Repair the smallest applicable control, test with a least-privilege session and verify both allowed and intentionally denied operations across the affected accounts.

Analogy. Account policies set the building rules; IAM grants individual access cards.

StackSets: one template, separate target stacks 
Common template → StackSet → selected account × Region stacks → per-target status

Each selected account–Region combination receives its own stack/resources. Region order and account concurrency control rollout; console, CLI/API and IaC can configure it.

StackSets replicate one template definition, with supported parameter overrides. They are not a general dependency orchestrator for unrelated templates. Check target roles, capabilities and resource naming before broad rollout.

Target accountSydneyMelbourne
DevelopmentOwn stack/resourcesOwn stack/resources
ProductionOwn stack/resourcesOwn stack/resources
aws cloudformation list-stack-instances --stack-set-name baseline

Exam trigger. Apply the same baseline to many account–Region targets → StackSets.

Common trap. A single StackSet operation does not create one global stack or one shared copy of every resource.

Official references: StackSets

AWS references: SCPs · RAM · Identity Center

IAM access investigation

Separate authentication, role trust and permission to perform an action on a resource.

Flow. Principal → trusted session → action/resource/context evaluation → allowed or denied operation.

  • Identity policies grant actions to identities; resource policies grant supported resource access. Trust policies control role assumption. Cross-account access generally needs trust/resource permission and caller-side permission as applicable.
  • Explicit deny wins. Permissions boundaries, session policies and SCPs limit permissions; they do not independently grant them. Resource-policy evaluation has principal-specific exceptions: inspect the actual principal/session.
  • Use roles with temporary credentials and MFA/federation for people. IAM Access Analyzer identifies supported external/unused access; the policy simulator helps test policies but is not a full live request.
  • Inspect conditions such as source ARN/account, requested Region, tags, VPC endpoint and MFA. A valid credential does not bypass a missing network route.

Choose / compare. Cannot assume role → check caller permission and target trust; session exists but action denied → inspect action/resource, limits, conditions and relevant resource policy.

Try the related local exercise: access

Exam clue. A user authenticated successfully yet receives AccessDenied → investigate authorisation, not a password reset.

Trap. An execution role controls what code calls; it does not automatically allow a service to invoke that code. A network filter cannot grant IAM access.

Example 
aws sts get-caller-identity
aws sts decode-authorization-message --encoded-message ENCODED_MESSAGE
# Requires sts:DecodeAuthorizationMessage; inspect returned decision context.
Investigate, remediate & verify

Evidence. Start with sts get-caller-identity, exact denied action/resource and CloudTrail error. Decode an encoded authorisation message with STS when present and authorised.

Action → verification. Correct narrowly scoped policies, then retry the precise operation and test a prohibited operation. Avoid attaching AdministratorAccess as an investigation shortcut.

Analogy. Trust admits a visitor; permissions specify rooms; guardrails limit the entire visit.

Cross-account S3 copy: keep one identity with both permissions 
Finance credentials → CopyObject(destination Finance, source HR/Audit)
Same credentials must pass source GetObject AND destination PutObject

Direct access can combine Finance identity-policy permissions with HR/Audit bucket policies granting the Finance principal source reads. Identity policies attach to users/groups/roles; bucket policies attach to buckets.

AssumeRole returns a different role session. It does not union the original Finance user’s permissions with the HR role’s permissions. A role needs trust for assumption and permissions for the actual source/destination operations.

This example assumes same-partition general-purpose buckets and isolates policy evaluation. Object ownership, explicit denies, organisation controls and any SSE-KMS permissions can add requirements.

# Excerpt: run with the intended Finance profile; review all policies first
aws s3api copy-object --profile finance --bucket finance-archive \
  --key audit/report.csv --copy-source audit-source/report.csv

Exam trigger. Copy across accounts while retaining existing Finance writes → grant direct source access to that Finance identity.

Common trap. Assuming a source-account role does not automatically carry the original identity’s destination write permission.

Official references: Copy permissions · Role session permissions

AWS references: Policy evaluation · Access Analyzer

Config & continuous compliance

Record supported resource configuration changes and evaluate configured compliance rules.

Flow. Supported resource configuration → recorder → rule evaluation → safe remediation → re-evaluation.

  • A recorder captures supported resource types in its configured scope; rules evaluate recorded configuration or periodic conditions. An aggregator collects multi-account/Region views; it does not replace source recorders.
  • Conformance packs group rules and remediation definitions. Automatic remediation requires configured permissions and safe assumptions; stale evaluations can trigger inappropriate action.
  • CloudTrail records the API actor, while Config records the resource’s configuration history. Artifact supplies AWS compliance documents, not continuous auditing of your workload.
  • Implement supplied classification and compliance requirements through tags, resource selection, encryption and approved Regions/services; do not invent the organisation’s policy.

Choose / compare. Need history/compliance of a resource property → Config; need who changed it → CloudTrail.

Exam clue. Continuously identify unencrypted supported resources → Config rule/conformance pack.

Trap. An aggregator is a view, not automatic recording or repair. A compliant rule result only proves that rule’s evaluated condition.

Example 
aws configservice describe-compliance-by-config-rule \
  --compliance-types NON_COMPLIANT
aws configservice describe-configuration-recorder-status
Investigate, remediate & verify

Evidence. Check recorder status, resource support/scope, delivery errors, rule triggers, evaluation timestamp and remediation execution output.

Action → verification. Correct the resource through managed configuration, re-evaluate and verify COMPLIANT plus the actual setting. Adjust permissions/preconditions to prevent remediation loops.

Analogy. A property inspection log, compared with a checklist at each relevant change.

AWS references: Config · Conformance packs

KMS, encryption & secrets

Control cryptographic key use separately from access to encrypted data.

Flow. Encrypted data key → authorised KMS Decrypt → recovered data key → local/service data decryption.

  • SSE-S3 uses S3-managed keys; SSE-KMS uses KMS-protected data keys. A customer-managed KMS key offers policy/lifecycle control. SSE-C supplies a key to S3 over HTTPS; client-side encryption happens before upload.
  • Envelope encryption protects large data locally with a data key; KMS protects that key. GenerateDataKey returns plaintext and encrypted representations; the application stores the encrypted one and protects/clears plaintext.
  • A KMS key policy is essential; IAM permission only works when the key policy permits that mechanism. Cross-account key use needs appropriate key-policy and identity permissions. Check key Region, state, grants and encryption context.
  • Secrets Manager stores and rotates supported credentials; Parameter Store SecureString protects named configuration. Rotation must update dependent applications and connectivity correctly.

Choose / compare. Object read allowed but SSE-KMS decryption denied → check key access as well as S3. Key rotation does not require re-encrypting every object and does not fix an access policy.

ModeKey / encryption responsibilityOperational check
SSE-S3S3 manages keys; S3 encryptsS3 permissions and resulting object mode.
SSE-KMSKMS-protected data key; S3 encryptsObject access plus applicable KMS policy/state/context.
SSE-CCustomer sends key over HTTPS; S3 encryptsCustomer retains key; S3 does not persist it; no inherent KMS dependency.
Client-side encryptionClient encrypts before uploadClient key recovery/libraries; S3 receives ciphertext.

Try the related local exercise: access

Exam clue. S3 GetObject permission succeeds but encrypted object remains unreadable → KMS policy/state/context investigation.

Trap. KMS permissions do not grant S3 access; S3 permissions do not automatically grant KMS use. GenerateDataKeyWithPlaintext is not an API.

Example 
aws kms describe-key --key-id KEY_ARN
aws kms get-key-policy --key-id KEY_ARN --policy-name default
# Inspect policy; do not print secrets or plaintext data keys into logs.
Investigate, remediate & verify

Evidence. Inspect the exact KMS error, CloudTrail key operation, key ARN/state, key policy, caller IAM policy, grants and encryption context. A disabled/deleting key can make data unavailable.

Action → verification. Restore approved key access/state, retry a controlled decrypt/read and verify expected denies. Test a rotated secret with the dependent service before marking rotation complete.

Analogy. Access to the locked cabinet and permission to use its key are separate checks.

Encrypted ASG launches: authorise the service-linked role 
AMI + encrypted snapshot → ASG service-linked role → KMS authorisation → fresh encrypted volume
Application instance profile acts later, after the instance boots.

For a customer-managed key in the ASG account, grant the ASG service-linked role the documented key-use and grant-creation permissions. Giving only the instance application role decrypt access does not authorise image launch.

For a key owned by another account, AWS’s ASG workflow requires the key policy plus an explicit KMS grant for the ASG service-linked role. An authorised principal creates that grant; this is not a cross-account AssumeRole flow.

Copying/re-encrypting the image under a key in the consuming account is an alternative, not mandatory. A question that omits key ownership is missing the deciding condition; do not silently assume another account.

A missing launch-key permission can surface as generic Client.InternalError. Check the ASG service-linked role (normally AWSServiceRoleForAutoScaling), source key ownership and scaling activity. EC2/EBS creates a new virtual volume; data keys encrypt blocks and KMS keys protect those data keys. Exact KMS operations depend on source-snapshot encryption.

Key ownerRelevant controlNot sufficient
Same ASG accountDocumented key policy for ASG service-linked roleOnly the application instance profile
Different accountKey policy + explicit grant for ASG service-linked roleAssumeRole alone or AMI launch permission alone

Exam trigger. Encrypted ASG launch fails before application startup → inspect the service-linked role, key owner, policy and required grant.

Common trap. A role trust policy, an application-role Allow and a KMS grant are different controls.

Official references: AWS ASG key policy and grant examples

AWS references: KMS policies · Data keys · Secrets rotation

ACM & encrypted connections

Maintain trusted certificates and TLS configuration at the actual termination point.

Flow. Domain validation → suitable ACM certificate → correct listener/endpoint → validated TLS connection.

  • ALB HTTPS listeners need a suitable certificate in the load balancer’s Region. A CloudFront viewer certificate from ACM must be in us-east-1.
  • Check SAN/hostname match, expiry, validation status, chain and listener security policy. Eligible ACM-managed renewal relies on continued validation and service use.
  • Viewer-to-edge TLS and edge/load-balancer-to-origin TLS are separate connections. Encrypting one leg does not prove the backend leg is protected.

Choose / compare. Need certificate lifecycle → ACM; need encryption keys for stored data → KMS. DNS validation proves domain control, not application health.

Exam clue. Browser certificate mismatch → hostname/certificate/listener investigation before changing IAM.

Trap. A valid certificate in the wrong Region cannot be attached to the ALB. CloudFront’s viewer certificate Region is a special requirement.

Example 
openssl s_client -connect api.example.com:443 -servername api.example.com </dev/null
# Diagnostic command; inspect certificate dates, chain and hostname separately.
Investigate, remediate & verify

Evidence. Inspect the certificate actually served with SNI, DNS record, listener binding, validation records and origin hostname/trust.

Action → verification. Attach/renew the correct certificate and policy, then test hostname validation and both connection legs. Retain DNS validation records for managed renewal.

Analogy. A certificate is a verified identity document for a particular connection endpoint.

AWS references: ACM · CloudFront certificates

Security findings & classification

Interpret the finding type, prioritise impact and verify the relevant corrective control.

Flow. Specialist assessment → finding → prioritised investigation → corrective control → reassessment.

  • GuardDuty detects threats from supported data sources; Inspector assesses supported workload vulnerabilities/exposure; Macie discovers sensitive S3 data.
  • Security Hub aggregates/prioritises supported findings and security posture checks. Config evaluates configuration compliance. Trusted Advisor provides supported advisory checks; availability depends on plan/feature.
  • Apply the supplied data classification to access, encryption, retention and logging. A classification label without enforcement does not protect data.
  • Current guide terminology includes AWS Security Agent; its docs now describe it as part of AWS Continuum. It supports application security review/threat modelling/penetration testing, not a replacement for runtime threat detection.

Choose / compare. Vulnerable package → Inspector; suspicious activity → GuardDuty; sensitive S3 content → Macie; aggregate findings → Security Hub.

Exam clue. Central view of findings from several supported security services → Security Hub.

Trap. A suppressed or archived finding is not proof of remediation. AWS Artifact reports describe AWS controls, not your instance’s patch status.

Example 
# Inspector example: list findings for inspection, then filter to the affected resource
aws inspector2 list-findings --max-results 10
Investigate, remediate & verify

Evidence. Read resource/account/Region, evidence, severity, last observation and workflow status. Confirm the affected running artifact and possible exposure before dismissing a finding.

Action → verification. Patch/isolate/restrict according to the approved runbook; rescan and verify runtime version, connectivity and finding state. Preserve investigation evidence.

Analogy. Different inspectors check different hazards; the central register does not perform every inspection.

AWS references: Security Hub · Inspector · Security Agent / Continuum

VPC routes, subnets & filters

Provide address space, routing and traffic controls for VPC-associated workloads.

Subnet IPs · 5 reserved addresses

In a standard IPv4 subnet, AWS reserves the first four addresses and the last address. Example: 10.0.0.0/24 has 256 − 5 = 251 assignable addresses.

Reserved addressPurpose
10.0.0.0Network address
10.0.0.1VPC router
10.0.0.2AWS DNS reservation
10.0.0.3Future use
10.0.0.255Broadcast address (VPC broadcast is unsupported)

The DNS resolver is at primary VPC CIDR + 2; every subnet’s +2 is still reserved. BYOIP has exceptions. Standard IPv6 subnets also reserve the first four and last address. AWS reference.

Flow. Source → route → applicable filters → target listener → permitted return path.

  • A VPC is regional; a subnet belongs to one AZ. Plan non-overlapping CIDRs, free subnet IPs and routes. A public subnet has an internet-gateway route; an instance also needs appropriate addressing and filters for IPv4 internet access.
  • Route tables select paths; longest-prefix matching matters. Security groups are stateful allow filters on ENIs; NACLs are stateless ordered allow/deny filters at subnet boundaries.
  • IPv4 private egress commonly uses NAT; an egress-only internet gateway handles outbound-initiated IPv6 internet connections. For zonal NAT deployments, align AZ paths to avoid a dependency on another AZ and unnecessary transfer.
  • Peering is non-transitive and needs routes on both sides. Transit Gateway connects supported networks through attachments and associated/propagated route tables. These paths still need security controls.

Choose / compare. An IAM denial needs policy analysis; a timeout needs DNS/routes/filters/target checks. A route does not grant application authorisation.

ControlMechanismReturn path
Security groupStateful; allow rules on ENIsAllowed established-flow return is tracked.
NACLStateless; ordered allow/deny at subnetExplicit request and ephemeral return rules.
Route tableDestination-prefix path selectionDestination must have a valid return route too.
DNSName → address / endpointA correct answer does not prove TCP connectivity.

Try the related local exercise: network

Exam clue. Request arrives but response is blocked with stateless filtering → inspect ephemeral return-port rules.

Trap. A NAT gateway does not accept unsolicited inbound internet connections. An internet-gateway route alone does not assign a public IP.

Example 
# Return path illustration, not firewall syntax
browser:54321 → ALB:443
ALB:443 → browser:54321
# NACLs must permit the relevant destination ports in both directions.
Investigate, remediate & verify

Evidence. Trace DNS → source subnet route → gateway/attachment → destination route → SG/NACL → listener → return path. Check overlapping CIDRs and subnet address exhaustion.

Action → verification. Correct the specific route/filter/address issue, test from the affected source and verify both request and response. Restrict the fix to required peers/ports.

Analogy. Routes are roads; firewalls are gates; DNS is the address book.

Same VPC: a route is not permission 
App ENI → subnet route table’s local path → DB ENI
                      then applicable SG / NACL checks → database port

A VPC is Regional; a subnet occupies one AZ. Each subnet has one associated route table, while a table can serve several subnets. Tables automatically have local routes for the VPC CIDRs; separate same-VPC subnets normally already have a routing path.

That path does not authorise the connection. A typical EC2 → RDS connection needs the DB security group to allow the database port from the app security group, plus permitted NACL/return traffic. SGs apply to ENIs/resources; NACLs apply at subnet boundaries.

IPv4 and IPv6 CIDRs are separate address spaces. IPv6 assignment is optional; an EC2 instance does not automatically receive IPv6 merely because it exists in a VPC.

Exam trigger. Same-VPC SQL timeout with a valid local route → check DB ingress, NACLs and the listener before adding routing infrastructure.

Common trap. Different subnets do not, by themselves, mean private instances or blocked inter-subnet routing.

Official references: Route tables · Security controls

New versus default security controls 
Route exists → verify the actual rules → test request AND return traffic

These are initial defaults, not a substitute for inspecting the current configuration. The default security group’s self-reference covers resources assigned to that group; it is not a blanket inbound allow from the whole VPC.

Control at creationInboundOutbound
New custom SGNo allow rulesAll outbound initially
Default SGFrom resources using itselfAll outbound initially
Default NACLAllow trafficAllow traffic
New custom NACLDeny until configuredDeny until configured

Exam trigger. A newly created custom NACL can block a routed connection before any application code runs.

Common trap. “Default security group” and “new custom security group” have different initial inbound rules.

Official references: Default SG · Default NACL

IGW, NAT and egress-only IGW 
Direct IPv4: public IPv4/EIP + IGW route + filters
Private IPv4: private instance → public NAT → IGW
Outbound-only IPv6: IPv6 instance → egress-only IGW

For direct IPv4 internet access, an IGW route alone is insufficient: the instance also needs public IPv4 addressing and suitable rules. A public NAT gateway lets private IPv4 clients initiate connections and receive replies.

An egress-only IGW is IPv6-only: it permits outbound-initiated flows and their replies while preventing new internet-initiated connections. It does not translate IPv4 or assign IPv6 addresses.

Exam trigger. Outbound-only IPv6 requirement → egress-only IGW; private IPv4 egress → suitable NAT path.

Common trap. A public subnet route does not automatically attach a public address to every instance.

Official references: Egress-only IGW · Internet gateway

Public address does not prove public-internet transit 
AWS public IP → AWS global network → AWS public IP (documented exceptions)
Private IP + configured peering routes → private-address path

Current AWS documentation says AWS-originating/AWS-destined public-IP traffic stays on its global network, except traffic to/from China Regions and the European Sovereign Cloud Region.

Inter-Region peering supplies private addressing/routes over the AWS backbone. Merely creating peering does not reroute calls still addressed to public IPs. Routes, permissions, addressing and TLS remain separate checks.

Exam trigger. Need private addressing → private connectivity/routes; do not use an outdated public-IP transit explanation.

Common trap. Edge locations and Direct Connect are not automatically inserted into an ordinary EC2-to-EC2 request.

Official references: VPC network behaviour

AWS references: Routes · SG vs NACL · NAT

Endpoints & private connectivity

Reach supported services privately with the correct endpoint and DNS/routing model.

Flow. Signed service request → gateway route or interface ENI → AWS service; permissions remain separate.

  • Gateway endpoints support S3 and DynamoDB using route-table entries and service prefix lists; they do not create application-subnet ENIs and have no additional endpoint charge.
  • Interface endpoints use PrivateLink ENIs in selected subnets/AZs with security groups and optional private DNS. They typically charge hourly and for data processing.
  • An endpoint policy limits applicable access; it does not replace IAM, resource or KMS policies. S3 supports gateway and interface models with different reachability/use cases.
  • Troubleshoot existing Site-to-Site VPN/Client VPN and hybrid routes with tunnel status, BGP/static routes, DNS forwarding and filters. Consider Transit Gateway/peering path and return routing; do not assume transitive peering.

Choose / compare. Private EC2 to S3/DynamoDB in the same Region/VPC context → gateway endpoint is often sufficient; supported private API access via ENIs → interface endpoint.

EndpointNetwork representationKey decision
GatewayRoute-table prefix-list targetS3/DynamoDB; no additional endpoint charge; not a transitive hybrid doorway.
InterfacePrivateLink ENIs + SGs in selected subnetsSupported APIs/private DNS; hourly and processing charges.

Try the related local exercise: network

Exam clue. No NAT needed for private S3 access from the workload VPC → suitable S3 gateway endpoint.

Trap. Gateway endpoints are not transitive through peering/TGW for remote clients. Registering an endpoint does not authorise every API operation.

Example 
aws ec2 describe-vpc-endpoints --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=vpc-0123456789abcdef0
# Gateway: S3 prefix-list route; interface: HTTPS → private ENI.
Investigate, remediate & verify

Evidence. Check service/Region, private DNS, VPC DNS settings, endpoint SG:443, route-table association, endpoint policy and caller/resource permissions.

Action → verification. Correct routing/DNS/access, test the service API from the private workload and confirm the actual endpoint path. Compare endpoint and NAT costs for traffic volume and AZ placement.

Analogy. A private doorway still needs a working road, the correct address and an access card.

AWS references: S3 gateway endpoints · Interface endpoints · VPN troubleshooting

Route 53 & DNS operations

Resolve names and choose DNS answers according to the configured routing and health policy.

Flow. Name query → appropriate resolver/zone → routing policy → DNS answer; application traffic follows separately.

  • Public hosted zones answer internet DNS; private hosted zones require appropriate VPC association/resolution. Check delegation, record type/name and split-horizon behaviour.
  • Failover supports primary/secondary answers; weighted splits DNS answers; latency selects suitable regional endpoints. Health checks and EvaluateTargetHealth affect eligible answers, subject to policy behaviour.
  • Route 53 Resolver inbound/outbound endpoints and forwarding rules support hybrid name resolution. Allow DNS traffic and avoid forwarding loops; log queries to investigate actual names/responses. Current documentation calls the VPC service Route 53 VPC Resolver; the exam guide also uses the older Resolver name.
  • DNS Firewall filters supported Resolver queries by domain rules. WAF filters HTTP requests, Shield addresses DDoS protection and Network Firewall filters network traffic; their boundaries differ.

Choose / compare. Name fails but IP works → DNS investigation. Static global IP entry and supported endpoint failover → Global Accelerator may fit better than DNS changes.

Exam clue. Only on-premises clients cannot resolve a private AWS name → inspect Resolver inbound path and conditional forwarding.

Trap. DNS supplies an address; the application request is a separate connection. Weighted DNS does not guarantee a precise per-request percentage.

Example 
dig api.example.com
dig @VPC_RESOLVER_IP internal.example.com
# Use a real reachable resolver IP; compare answer, status and TTL.
Investigate, remediate & verify

Evidence. Use dig from the affected network; inspect authoritative answers, TTL/cache, hosted-zone association, Resolver rules, endpoint SGs and health-check results.

Action → verification. Repair delegation/record/forwarding, then verify from public and private clients after appropriate cache expiry. DNS failover is not instant active-connection migration.

Analogy. An address book can choose a branch, but it does not carry the visitor to that branch.

AWS references: Routing policies · Resolver · DNS Firewall

CloudFront & Global Accelerator

Operate global delivery with the right cache, origin and failover behaviour.

Flow. Viewer → CloudFront cache hit or configured origin; Global Accelerator is an alternative traffic-entry pattern.

  • CloudFront caches eligible HTTP content at edge locations. Behaviours choose origins by path; a cache key distinguishes query strings/headers/cookies that genuinely change the response.
  • An origin group supplies primary/secondary failover for GET, HEAD and OPTIONS under configured failure conditions; it does not merge responses. TTL changes cannot fix a missing language/tenant cache-key dimension.
  • CloudFront Functions handles lightweight supported viewer transformations; Lambda@Edge supports broader request/response processing. Dynamic content alone does not require edge code.
  • Global Accelerator provides static anycast IP entry and routes supported TCP/UDP application traffic to healthy endpoints over the AWS network; it is not an HTTP object cache.

Choose / compare. Cache HTTP responses/static S3 images → CloudFront; stable global IPs and endpoint routing → Global Accelerator. Compare transfer, request, invalidation and accelerator charges.

CapabilityChoose forCommon mistake
CloudFront behaviours / originsPath-based HTTP content sources and cachingTreating every origin as a failover target.
CloudFront origin groupConfigured primary/secondary read-request failoverAssuming general POST replay or merged responses.
CloudFront Functions / Lambda@EdgeRequired supported custom request/response workAssuming dynamic content always requires edge code.
Global AcceleratorStatic anycast entry + supported endpoint routingTreating it as an HTTP object cache.

Exam clue. Wrong language served from cache → cache key; need a stable global anycast entry → Global Accelerator.

Trap. Forwarding a parameter to the origin and including it in the cache key are distinct choices. Origin failover is not general write-request replay.

Example 
# Conceptual cache keys
/reviews?lang=en → /reviews|lang=en
/reviews?lang=ja → /reviews|lang=ja
# Include lang in cache policy if it changes the origin response.
Investigate, remediate & verify

Evidence. Inspect DNS, viewer/origin TLS, behaviour match, cache policy, origin request policy, status/error caching, origin health and relevant access/WAF logs.

Action → verification. Correct the policy/origin rather than repeatedly lowering TTL; invalidate when appropriate, then test cache hit/miss and response correctness for distinct request variants.

Analogy. CloudFront is a local copy desk; Global Accelerator is a globally advertised entrance to the application.

Origin Shield consolidates cache misses 
Viewer → edge → Regional edge cache → selected Origin Shield → origin
                                (applicable bypass/routing exceptions)

Origin Shield is an additional AWS-managed CloudFront caching layer in a selected Region, not an ElastiCache cluster you deploy. It consolidates eligible origin-bound misses from caching layers.

Choose the supported Shield Region with the lowest latency to the origin. Weighted DNS can distribute traffic but does not inherently consolidate repeated misses or improve cache reuse.

Exam trigger. Many cache locations request the same uncached object → evaluate Origin Shield for origin-load reduction.

Common trap. The typical cache hierarchy has exceptions; do not promise every request always traverses every cache layer.

Official references: Origin Shield

S3 REST origin versus website custom origin 
Preferred private origin: CloudFront OAC → signed S3 REST request → restrictive bucket policy
Website endpoint: CloudFront custom origin → HTTP website request

OAC is preferred over legacy OAI for supported S3 REST origins. S3 website endpoints are custom origins: neither OAC nor OAI applies, and the website endpoint supports HTTP only.

A configured secret Referer header checked by a bucket policy is a limited website-origin workaround. Headers can be spoofed; this is not equivalent to authenticated OAC access. For robust CloudFront-only access, use the REST endpoint with appropriate OAC and bucket restrictions.

Exam trigger. Private S3 content accessible only through a distribution → REST origin + OAC + scoped bucket policy.

Common trap. Changing an origin label does not turn a website endpoint into a REST endpoint or add HTTPS support.

Official references: OAC / OAI restrictions · Website endpoint differences · Referer limitations

Endpoint location versus SigV4 signing Region 
CloudFront (global) → request signed for Sydney
                         bucket now in Singapore → 400 AuthorizationHeaderMalformed

The origin endpoint directs the request; the SigV4 authorisation scope authenticates it and includes a Region. S3 must accept that signing Region. It is not merely a routing field in a JSON body.

Deleting a bucket and recreating its name in another Region can leave stale origin/signing information in a distribution. Confirm the actual bucket Region, update/re-save the CloudFront origin and allow deployment to finish, then retest.

CloudFront distributions are global and access keys do not have a home Region. An explicit wrong-Region S3 response proves an HTTP exchange occurred; it is different from a network timeout.

# Illustrative credential scope, not credentials or an executable request
Credential=<access-key-id>/<date>/ap-southeast-2/s3/aws4_request
# Compare the Region with what the actual S3 bucket expects.

Exam trigger. S3 explicitly says the signing Region is wrong → investigate origin metadata and request scope, not CloudFront’s supposed home Region.

Common trap. The bucket was deleted/recreated, not moved in place. Broader bucket permissions do not repair a malformed signing scope.

Official references: AWS wrong-signing-Region recovery

AWS references: Cache keys · Origin failover · Global Accelerator

Network evidence & protection

Identify the failing hop with configuration analysis, flow records and measured network health.

Flow. Configuration model / flow record / live probe → evidence → targeted check → real traffic verification.

  • VPC Flow Logs describe supported IP traffic metadata and ACCEPT/REJECT decisions; they are not packet payload captures and are not instantaneous.
  • Reachability Analyzer models supported configuration paths without sending packets. A reachable model does not prove the application is listening or healthy.
  • CloudWatch Internet Monitor observes internet-path performance for configured resources; Network Synthetic Monitor probes supported hybrid paths for latency/loss. Network Flow Monitor provides supported workload flow/performance visibility.
  • Use ALB/CloudFront access logs for HTTP status and timing, WAF logs for rule decisions and container logs for application/network startup faults. Audit WAF, Shield, DNS Firewall and Network Firewall at their own inspection boundaries.

Choose / compare. Configuration block → Reachability Analyzer; actual accepted/rejected IP flow → Flow Logs; internet/hybrid degradation → the relevant CloudWatch network monitor.

Exam clue. Need to locate a configured network block without probing production → Reachability Analyzer.

Trap. Flow Logs ACCEPT is not HTTP 200. A trace gap can be sampling/instrumentation rather than a network failure.

Example 
# Illustrative Flow Log excerpt, simplified
srcaddr=10.0.11.20 dstaddr=10.0.21.30 dstport=5432 protocol=6 action=REJECT
# Inspect relevant SG/NACL configuration; record alone does not identify the exact rule.
Investigate, remediate & verify

Evidence. Correlate source/destination IPs, ports, protocol, direction and time. Interpret ACCEPT as filter acceptance, not business success; verify route symmetry and DNS separately.

Action → verification. Repair the first proven failing dependency, retest actual connectivity/application response and compare before/after latency, loss and log outcomes.

Analogy. A road map, a traffic register and a timed test drive answer different questions.

AWS references: Flow Logs · Reachability Analyzer · Network Synthetic Monitor

Health & assisted investigation

Use service health and assisted analysis as evidence within an accountable operational process.

Flow. Incident → affected scope → connected evidence → reviewed hypothesis → approved repair → verification.

  • AWS Health provides relevant service/account event information; compare affected Region/resources with your own telemetry rather than assuming every failure is AWS-wide.
  • AWS DevOps Agent correlates connected operational evidence and deployment context to investigate incidents and recommend improvements. Scope integrations/roles and validate conclusions against logs and metrics.
  • Kiro assists with code/configuration and troubleshooting workflows. Review generated commands and changes; an assistant recommendation is not a verified root cause or an approved production change.
  • Monitor AI workloads as workloads: access, model/API quotas, errors, latency, cost and sensitive logging. Bedrock being in scope does not turn SOA-C03 into model-training certification.

Choose / compare. Suspected AWS service disruption → AWS Health plus resource telemetry; cross-signal investigation → assisted tooling with least-privilege evidence access.

Exam clue. Current guide names Kiro/DevOps Agent: know their investigation/automation role, not an invented replacement for monitoring.

Trap. The June 2026 guide revision matters; older SOA-C02 service lists omit newer capabilities. Validate service names/features against current docs.

Example 
# Investigation checklist (conceptual)
symptom → affected account/Region/AZ → evidence → hypothesis
→ approved action → user-visible verification → prevention
Investigate, remediate & verify

Evidence. Check the affected scope, linked telemetry, permissions and recent changes. Identify what evidence supports each hypothesis and what test would disprove it.

Action → verification. Execute the approved bounded repair, verify user-visible recovery and record evidence. Treat recommendations as inputs to change control, not automatic proof.

Analogy. An experienced assistant can propose a diagnosis; measurements and a recovery test establish the outcome.

Quota recommendation or application investigation? 
Trusted Advisor check status → EventBridge us-east-1 → SNS
Application telemetry → trace map / older ServiceLens → investigate dependency

Trusted Advisor evaluates supported environment checks across cost, security, resilience, performance, operational excellence and quotas. Service-limit checks flag 80% yellow and 100% red; results are snapshots, not live throughput measurements.

Kinesis shard-count quota is distinct from IncomingBytes/IncomingRecords and throughput-exceeded metrics. Trace correlation needs configured/instrumented telemetry; it does not invent a latency target.

Trusted Advisor events are best effort in us-east-1. Current documentation requires Business Support+, Enterprise Support or Unified Operations for this EventBridge integration; older exam material uses earlier plan names.

QuestionUseEvidence
Which dependency is slow?Trace map / ServiceLens terminologyInstrumented request spans, logs, metrics
Are supported quotas nearly used?Trusted Advisor / Service QuotasConfiguration/usage and supported check
Are records being throttled?Kinesis CloudWatch metricsPer-shard/stream throughput and errors

Exam trigger. Quota utilisation warning → supported quota check; slow checkout dependency → metrics/logs/traces.

Common trap. A shard-count quota increase does not itself fix a hot partition key or per-shard throughput throttling.

Official references: Trusted Advisor · Quota criteria · Events / plan eligibility

AWS references: AWS Health · DevOps Agent · Kiro
